speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
that Bill C-40, an Act to amend the Old Age Security Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.
She said: Mr. Speaker, let me say, first of all, that I certainly appreciate the healthy applause rising up from the Opposition benches. This augurs well for the debate on this Bill! I assume that Members will vote unanimously in favour of what will probably be the last Bill we shall be proposing in support of the Guaranteed Income Supplement, because once this Bill is passed, from then on all senior citizens will necessarily be above the poverty line.

As you know, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-40 is basically focused on adding, in two slices, a full $50 a month, on top of the usual indexation, to what we call in the jargon "single pensioners" receiving the supplement. That means hundreds of thousands of seniors who are widows, widowers, single, separated, divorced and so on, who have no means or very little income other than what we call the "public pensions".
That is what this Bill is intended to do. However, we took the opportunity-and I am really confident that we will obtain the support of all Hon. Members of this House-to make other changes which will improve the pension system at the same time. These are small changes affecting perhaps 3,000 or even as few as 50 people a year. These are Canadians who for some technical reason fall between two chairs when it comes to the guaranteed income supplement. This, in a way, is a means to an end, and it is a happy end because it is the end to a very unhappy situation.
Some seniors, because of the limitations of, I suppose, the social sciences in preceding decades, still suffer a lot by not having a basic income guaranteed to them. Let me explain. In Canada, as in many other countries, I suppose-I would not know for sure until I researched the question-when we established the pension the concept was that a person who was
alone, for whatever reason, would receive half of what a couple receives. However, because of studies of family budgets and so on we now know that to live alone costs more than 50 per cent of a couple's needs. For example, the basic one-bedroom apartment, hydro and telephone will cost the same for a person alone as for a couple. Therefore, many groups-and in all fairness we should refer to them right now in this House-such as the Royal Commission on the Status of Pensions in Ontario, the Canadian Council on Social Development, the Senate Committee on Poverty and, I believe, the National Council on Welfare, have advocated that pensioners living alone and in need receive 60 per cent or a little more-which is what they are going to receive-of the budget of a couple.
That is why-and I do not say it in apology but in explanation-the couples who receive the supplement will not at this time receive a special increase. They will receive their usual indexation in July, next month. It is those, however, who are single and receive the supplement who will receive an additional $25 a month starting with their July cheque, and another additional $25 in their monthly cheques beginning in December. That, in a nutshell, is the purpose of this Bill.
I should mention that this increase will also be provided to widowed spouse's allowance recipients. Whatever their age or status, if they become widowed and they receive the spouse's allowance, which means they are younger than 65, which also means they are automatically in need, they will get the full $50 as well. In that way we are correcting what I would call a mistake of the past, of which I myself did not know. [Translation]
At this point I would like to say, Mr. Speaker, and I think it is very important, that my colleague, the Hon. Member from Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart), is to be commended for having brought this problem to the attention of the Government. When individuals receiving the spouse's allowance are widowed-and in most cases they are women-they do not receive the special increase for single persons because of a technicality in the Act. However, they are single, to all intents and purposes.
We are therefore correcting this, so that all widowed spouse allowance recipients will now receive the additional $50 provided in Bill C-40.1 think this is extremely important. [English]
I will make the point rapidly that many people who get this $50 are women. Unfortunately I do not have in my notes the exact percentage, but it is a majority and quite a high percentage. It reflects the make-up of society. The Hon. Member for

June 4, 1984
Old Age Security Act
Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), even if she is not always very nice to me when she speaks in this House, has joined forces with many of us to obtain changes in the pension system for homemakers. They raised the children, did unpaid voluntary work, or worked in the service industry or perhaps the small business enterprise of their husband, father or members of their family. They often had to work to help the family make ends meet without pay or with small pay and no private pension.
I also want to bring to the attention of Canadians that the group forming what we call the GIS pensioners, those who receive the supplement, are people in need. If they were younger than 65 they would be on welfare. We should not hide that fact from ourselves. We call it a supplement and there is no stigma attached to it, which I am very proud of. These people are in need and this Bill is not providing a luxury for them, it is a necessity.
To come back to this point of information, which I think should be shocking and shaking us all towards pension reform, the fact is that 235,000 single-rate pensioners in Canada have to receive the full supplement to the basic old age pension. That means they have absolutely nothing else in the way of income to live on during their old age. This is quite shocking for any country. It is dangerous as well because it means that a great number of Canadians, when they reach the so-called official age of retirement, will suffer quite a substantial fall in their standard of living. They may have their home paid for, especially in small towns or in rural Canada. However, in a city such as Montreal where 80 per cent of the people are tenants, they will not enjoy that benefit. That is a very worrying situation for the future and we want to address it.
Before moving to my next point I will explain something. The so-called single pensioners who get the supplement, even if only a partial supplement, will get the full additional $50, twice $25. People should know that. We are broadening the base of those who will get the supplement. There are those in the grey area of being very close to the poverty line. We are increasing the base. Our departmental estimates indicate that 25,000 old age pensioners who are not receiving any supplement will start to qualify immediately for a small supplement. They should check with my numerous offices all over the country and their local MPs to see whether they will qualify. These people have very little income and should apply.
Recognizing that single GIS pensioners are in need of better financial assistance was very important but in a way was not new. I will refer to the task force of parliamentarians of the three Parties who participated in what is now called the great pension debate. The task force on pension reform which studied the reform of private pensions also studied all pensions, including the two public pensions. For these GIS pensioners the task force recommended a special top-up benefit of $102 per month taxed back at 100 per cent in the lowest income group. Many Members and many Canadians think that would have been much better. However, it would have totally
changed the system. It would have been better for some but it would have eliminated a lot of GIS pensioners from receiving the supplement.
Let me explain why I did not recommend that to the Government. The reason is that the $102 per month with a tax back rate of 100 per cent would have given more money immediately to those who have nothing but the GIS. However, any pensioners receiving any money from another source would have that amount deducted from their GIS. That is a problem. As a Minister I could not talk with the task force on pension reform because it must operate independently, but I think it is fair that I explain today to the House and my colleagues why I did not recommend that to the Government.
Our system has two advantages which would have been lost by the recommendation of the task force report. One advantage of our present system is that it is proportionately adapted to each dollar of additional income from other sources. It is a fine graduation from those who receive the full OAS and the GIS with no other income to those with limited other income, and finally to those who have other income but not enough to match what is missing by even $10 a month and takes them over the poverty line. There is no disruption in this system; it is a scale that is finely tuned to the realities.
The second advantage is that we only take back 50 per cent of other income and thereby leave them 50 cents on the dollar. This means that we have built in within the public pension system in Canada incentives for people to build up their own savings. I do not know if I am turning into a capitalist, I do not think so, but I believe it is sacrosanct to build in and keep incentives for Canadians to save toward their older days.
Go ahead, become a capitalist.
That is John Turner's influence on you!

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Yes, but with a heart. That is the difference. We need the money to spend afterwards. We need a viable economy because I know how to spend the money.
Of course, we want jobs first and a good economy at the same time. Then we can refine our social programs to have the fantastic safety net about which Canadians are so pleased.
This being said, and despite the way Opposition is teasing me-I take it that it is all in friendship which, of course, is very dangerous when it comes from them-let me speak about the money which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) has provided in his Budget. In that Budget the Minister of Finance referred to the amount that this new program will cost. Of course, nothing can be established without a cost and I am proud that the Government saw fit to put aside, among its new expenditures, funds for two programs; jobs for young people in particular and funds for seniors in need to whom we have promised it as soon as the economy allows.
This year the increase will raise expenditures by $250 million. In the next fiscal year, 1985-86, there will be an additional cost of $460 million because the spending will be
June 4, 1984

over the full fiscal year. I am pleased that we are hearing less criticism that these are non-productive expenditures and that mine is a non-economic ministry. I am prepared to answer those criticisms.
That $250 million which we just added to the Budget and for which I am asking support at the second and final stages of this Bill will provide an additional $24 in the next month's cheque for single GIS pensioners. That money will return directly to the economy. It will be spent in the daily budget of those people and will return more rapidly to the economy than other savings as they meet their basic and immediate needs. It will increase consumer demand. In order to convince people that this is not wasted money, I can go as far as arguing that this expenditure of funds has an economic benefit that is equivalent to creating 3,000 new jobs this year and another 2,000 jobs next year. I suggest that there are not only social benefits to these social expenditures but economic benefits as well.
I am also asking Members to support the reform which this Act seeks to bring about. I think they will agree with it because we have taken a pragmatic approach to a problem that is typical of Canada as a country of immigrants.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make one comment, and I think you will understand, since you are from Quebec yourself. Dr. Camille Laurin, who is now the Quebec Minister for Social Affairs, after a rather stormy career with the Department of Education-and I hope he will not take the same kind of action in our social affairs field-Dr. Laurin has stated all of a sudden that he wants to patriate old age security pensions. In the course of my usual activities on the weekend, I spoke to quite a number of senior citizens groups. There were senior citizens from various parts of Quebec, and these people came to ask me, to plead with me to keep the pension so that I would be there to make sure there were no problems and the Province of Quebec did not make a hash of something that was working quite well. So I would like to reassure our senior citizens and say that this is a lot of rhetoric! There is no reason at all for patriating pensions. The system has always worked very well. I would rather not make any more political comments than I have to, but I must say that I am rather surprised at this Government, this separatist Government which not so long ago said through its Premier, Mr. Levesque, that senior citizens were a total loss, that it was their fault that the people who wanted Quebec to separate had lost the referendum and that senior citizens were holding Quebec hostage because they would not allow the province to separate, but on the other hand, they would all be dead in a few years and then we could have another referendum!
I would just like to say one thing. There will always be pensioners, there will always be senior citizens in Quebec, with the intelligence and discernment to realize what the advan-
Old Age Security Act
tages are for Quebec within Confederation. Therefore, despite Dr. Laurin's ideological dreams, old age pensions will stay where they are. If Dr. Laurin wants to give Quebec senior citizens more, or if he wants to give something to people between 60 and 64, he can do so right now. According to the Constitution, he does not need the permission of the federal Government and he does not even have to consult me, he can go ahead and do it. That is something we must not forget. Other provinces do it and refer to these additional payments as top-ups. Many provinces do this for their senior citizens.

I said we were also making a few other reforms to the system. One touches immigrants. Canada in that sense is a special country. We have immigrants who come here permanently. At the beginning of 1977 I became Minister of National Health and Welfare. That year we reformed the old age pension system for immigrants because Canada's rules were all or nothing. A person had to have many years of residence or he or she did not qualify. One did not have an image of the exact situation. Under my predecessor, who is now the Minister of Finance, amendments were brought in which changed the number of years of residence needed to qualify. The qualifications were more practical reflecting Canadian reality. We opened the door to all reciprocity agreements signed with other countries. Roughly one-third of our population comes from other countries. People who came from other countries had neither sufficient years of residence in their own country nor in Canada to qualify for a full pension. We organized a system allowing pensions to be brought from other countries which could then be combined with earned pension rights here.

Oh!-And since the Member for Kent (Mr. Bossy) who happens to be of Belgian origin is right next to me, I would like to say that on May 10 of this year, I signed the latest reciprocal agreement on old age security pensions in Brussels, at the Palais des comtes d'Egmont, an agreement which will make it possible for all Canadians of Belgian origin, immigrants of Belgian origin, and also people who decide to settle in Belgium, to qualify for their full pension, through the Canadian and Belgian governments. This is the sixth or seventh country with which we have signed an agreement, something that is very much appreciated, of course, by the Canadians concerned.

There was a downside to the 1977 amendments which favoured immigrants. I do not have the exact number of people affected, but a small number of Canadians of other origins do not qualify for pensions in Canada, or the GIS, for example. They do not qualify for x number of reasons. This could be aid to farmers in a person's native country not covered by any contributory plan. People could be in a situation in which they do not qualify for anything in their native land, nor in Canada. They literally fall between the two. This situation is being corrected by an amendment in Bill C-40. These people would

Old Age Security Act
be considered in a category of need. This does not open the door for people to send their older parents to Canada just to get the Canadian pension. That would not be realistic nor fair to other Canadians. But if people lived a certain number of years in Canada and are in need, they will be eligible to receive the full GIS or whatever part of the GIS they need.
There is another small change which is important. I am sure Members will all agree that each one of us is a social worker or an ombudsman in our ridings. We hear about and we see people who are outside of the system. Let me cite one case. [Translation]
Here, I would like to express my appreciation to the Hon. Member for Gamelin (Mr. Portelance), who brought the problem to my attention. I was not aware of this particular problem. The Hon. Member reasoned as follows: If the Government of Canada can go back five years to check income tax returns, and that is what happens if a person fails to pay income tax, since the Government has the authority to check returns over the last five years, then why shouldn't a person who did not know or did not apply for his old age security pension be entitled to retroactive payments for up to five years? Someone who is 71 or 70 or 69 is not entitled to retroactive payments for the years for which no application was made, although that person was unaware there was a pension. But we are changing that now.

To sum up, a person in Canada can receive only one year of retroactivity the way the system exists now.
I know of one case of three years.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
That is illegal. We will have to correct that case by some special mechanism. A person in Canada older than 65 years of age who does not know there is a system of public pensions for whatever reason and has not applied can only receive one year's benefits retroactively.
One such case was brought to the attention of the Hon. Member for Gamelin (Mr. Portelance) who brought it to my attention. He pleaded with very powerful reasoning. I promised that as soon as we had a Bill in the House, we would include this situation. According to my officials and what we know of the situation, we think there are 50 cases a year. That means 50 Canadians are not receiving their fair share.
We are also proposing that post-mortem applications for Old Age Security benefits be allowed in cases where the deceased would have been eligible for benefits had he or she applied. This provision would also give a widow or widower, if all the qualifications were met-the person could be a spouse's allowance case-entitlement to the spouse's allowance.
In a nutshell, Mr. Speaker, several other amendments are proposed in an effort to make the Old Age Security program more equitable and efficient. Included are provisions allowing for compensating pensioners who lose any benefit entitlement as a result of administrative error or erroneous advice. I think everybody will agree that such a change was needed. This Bill
will authorize when necessary the issuance of a certificate on presumption of death, repealing an unnecessary and potentially misleading provision dealing with benefit entitlement under international social security agreements. There are, of course, changes necessary to co-ordinate Canada Pension Plan benefits with other sources for GIS entitlement purposes. Members received the details of these amendments in the special information package we distributed to all Members in the House.
As my time is coming to an end, in conclusion I should like to call upon the new government, which we will form after the next election, to make a serious effort in the area of pension reform. Today I am talking about public pensions. Along with this provision, the law should be satisfactory for many decades because it brings all Canadians automatically above the poverty line. However, it is only above the poverty line. It is normal that the Government would not do more, in a sense, because Canadians should supplement that guaranteed tier of income, as it is often called, with their own private savings and, more important, with their company pensions. That is the image we should remember in Canada.
With Sweden we are the only countries in the world with decent universal public pensions. However, with the United States we are the worst countries of the industrialized world for not having private pensions. Approximately 55 per cent of Canadian workers, most of whom are women in the workforce, have no company pension. The others have pensions which are not portable, which do not have survivors' benefits, and which are not indexed in any way, shape or form to the cost of living. That is what I think should be the next step. We should put our own house in order in terms of Canada Pension Plan reforms which cannot be made without the agreement of a majority of the provinces with two-thirds of the population. Therefore, the Minister of Finance and myself are commencing discussions with the provinces toward that end. The best indicator of how good it is to live in a country is the way it treats its seniors, and I think every Member agrees with that.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, in commencing debate on Bill C-40, an Act to amend the Old Age Security Act, on behalf of the Progressive Conservative Party I want to say at the outset that we are in support of it. Not only do the major provisions of the Bill have our support, but they were recommended at various times through various opportunities by members of our Party.
That is my first point. My second point is that we do not intend to delay the Bill. We will co-operate not only in the debate on the Bill in terms of early and speedy passage but also raise certain issues which we believe should be addressed in the opportunity we now have in regard to pensions.
I point out to the House, and to the Minister specifically, that while we support the Bill there is a vast area of pension reform which we would have preferred to see addressed at this
June 4, 1984

point as well. However, that takes us into the question of a time frame with which I will deal in a few minutes. Those two points of view stand on the record, and I want the House to enter into this debate with them in mind.
Before getting into the main body of my remarks, I pay tribute to a number of my colleagues who have been in the forefront on behalf of our Party in pension and pension reform. While those of us who have specific responsibilities now in the areas of health and welfare have a personal concern, we have not had responsibility for the Party as has the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald). There is no other Member of the House-I would suggest no one in the country-who has developed over a period of time, not only through the process of time but because of dedication and keeping the matter in the forefront of issues, the issue of poverty among the elderly, especially the need to change the pension plan to address the economic reality faced by many of Canada's elderly women on a day to day basis. I pay tribute to her today.
Hear, hear!

In the latter part of my speech, as did the Minister, I want to talk about the task force on pension reform, and I will mention the work of other colleagues at that time.
It is important when we look at this Bill to let the Canadian public know at the outset what we in the House face at this point in time. Today, at the beginning of June, we have a Bill before us which received first reading on May 29. While I know the Government after first reading of the bill can come back with second reading very quickly, it is generally the process of the House that a period of time is allowed for private and collegial discussion after first reading and for groups in the country interested in the Bill's specific provisions to have an opportunity to look at them and come back with suggestions.
Pension reform-specifically the changes to the guaranteed income supplement-has been a point of discussion in the House for the last two years. On February 15, 1984 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) mentioned the $25 increase in his Budget to take effect on July 1, 1984 and the additional $25 in December, 1984. The Budget called for those provisions on February 15, but we only received the Bill for first reading on May 29 and today, on June 4, we are debating second reading. I am not trying to be difficult, but we have to be realistic about the situation. If we can get the Bill through the House reasonably quickly on second reading, it will go to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. At the present time that committee has before it Bill C-221, a Private Member's Bill in the name of the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) dealing with amendments to the Narcotics Act and the therapeutic use of heroin. As well it has Bill C-5, an Act to amend the Radiation Emitting Devices Act. All of us recognize that there will be a certain number of allotted days in June and that there is a certain political event
Old Age Security Act
which the Party opposite wants to conduct in Ottawa this month.
That being the case, we have very little opportunity in either the House or in committee to get a grip on pension reform and the discussion which I believe should take place. If I have any regret or criticism of the Minister, it is just that I would have preferred to see the Bill much earlier. Then we could have had it in committee and discussed its provisions over a longer period of time. Despite that difficulty, the two points which I made at the outset of my comments stand.
The major feature of the Bill is to increase the income of elderly pensioners who now receive the guaranteed income supplement. Of course, to receive the GIS is contingent upon reaching age 65 or being eligible for the Old Age Security Plan. That supplement will be increased by $25 per month in July of this year and by an additional $25 in December. We support that, but as I said a little more time would have been helpful.
It is interesting to note that the Minister-and I do not think I am being unkind-has some difficulty explaining some of the other provisions because they are complicated and require some study. For instance, there are changes to the War Veterans Act and changes affecting immigrants, just to name two. There is also the five-year period in which a person can now apply whereas in the past it was one year. These are all important details and I would suggest that time would have allowed us to bring forward better legislation than that which we have now.
That being the case, I would like to outline for the House who these people are who will be affected by the increase in the guaranteed income supplement of $25. Within the confines of the House of Commons, it is very easy to speak of this matter in general terms. However, who are these people who will be affected? As of March of this year, 2,490,000 Canadians over the age of 65 were receiving the basic universal old age pension which currently stands at $265.89 per month. If we take a look at those 2.5 million elderly Canadians, we would also discover that approximately 50 per cent, or 1,241,000 of them, qualified for some sort of guaranteed income supplement in March of this year. However, of that group, some 302,812 or 12.2 per cent qualified for the full supplement. The rest qualified for the partial supplement. There is no question that there are a number of elderly Canadians today who are not eligible for company pensions or who did not have the financial resources to build up private pensions and are solely dependent on the Old Age Security and the guaranteed income supplement.
In one of the last statements made by the Minister, she said that the increase to the GIS would raise the incomes of those single elderly people who are receiving both the Old Age Security and the guaranteed income supplement above the poverty line. I suggest that that is not correct. In fact, when looking at figures that we and others in this field have worked out, it is my submission that with the proposed changes once

June 4, 1984
Old Age Security Act
implemented, including both the $25 in July and the $25 in December, the 1984 incomes of single persons receiving OAS and GIS will be $6,625 per annum. That is still some $697 below the poverty line for those who live in rural areas and some $3,275 below the poverty line for those who live in urban areas.
I know that when we speak about the poverty line for rural and urban areas, we are using a basic figure or a norm. However, I suggest to the Minister and to her departmental officials that they re-examine the statement made by the Minister. I do not believe it is the case that these people who will be receiving income only from the OAS and the GIS will be placed above the poverty line after receiving these increases. Even taking into account the December increase, those people would still fall below the poverty line.
It is for that reason that a number of provinces have brought in programs generally on a quarterly basis to increase the pension for these people. In pension jargon, it is called a top-up of the pension plan. There is no question that the provinces have had to address that question in a financial way. I would suggest to the Minister that while we welcome these additions, part of her argument and her laudatory statements are not borne out in fact.
It is also important to note something which concerns me and that is that elderly Canadians who earned salaries which were relatively low as compared to salaries today and who did not have extra money to purchase pension plans or worked for companies that did not have pension plans now use a disproportionate amount of their income for basic necessities such as housing and food. I will not take the time of the House to mention figures, but there is no question that that is the case.
The Minister has said that the extra money from the GIS will flow back into the economy immediately because these people will spend it. That is true, but it is reflective of a more important issue. These people are spending higher percentages of their incomes on food, clothing and household necessities. Despite the adjustments for inflation, the fact remains that these people, on a day-by-day basis, still must face a very specific budgeting process which only they are able to undertake.
The whole question of the future of our society, a question of which pensions is but a part, is one which should concern us in this House and should concern all Canadians. While we welcome this Bill, I think there is a fundamental reality that we must face. I am not convinced that we are facing that reality as I had hoped that this Bill would. That reality is that social policy relating to such things as pensions, health care and the Canada Assistance Plan, to name just three, cannot be divorced from economic policy. It is that economic policy which I would like to address for a moment.
It is said, and it is true, that the Government of Canada must be deeply concerned about additional expenditures because of both the annualized deficit of some $30 million this year and the cumulative deficit of some $155 billion at the present time. That is the legacy of the Liberal Government. Today, more than one-quarter of the entire resources of the
Government of Canada are being spent not on debt repayment but on debt servicing. We as Canadians are now paying in excess of $20 billion for debt servicing. As is my bent, I will be conservative about it and say that if that amount could have been cut by 25 per cent through proper economic management, we would have had an additional $5 billion to put into pensions, health care, economic development or whatever the legitimate priorities of the Government may have been. Alternatively, we could have left that $5 billion in the hands of Canadians who could, with proper tax incentives, have bought pension plans on their own.
To put the situation into focus, at the present time the federal Government is spending approximately $9 billion on transfer payments through the block funding system for health care. If the debt servicing charge could have been reduced by $5 billion or 25 per cent, that amount would have been equal to 50 per cent of the total health care expenditures of the federal Government this year. That is why we cannot divorce economic policy from social policy.
We cannot afford to pay for social policies if our economic policies are not in place and properly managed. That is the dilemma and the legacy that I suggest is being left to elderly Canadians today and to generations to come. I say more in sorrow than in anger that that is the tragedy. When thinking of the potential of a country such as ours with people such as ours, one must recognize that we have unlimited opportunities relative to those of other nations. However, the deficit will affect social policy. No matter how much we want to be receptive to new plans and new expenditures and no matter how much we want the very best for our elderly, we must keep in mind that legacy. I condemn the Liberal Government for having foisted that legacy equally on the elderly and on future generations to come.
I spoke with a senior citizen this morning with respect to the Bill. I asked him what he would say if he had an opportunity to speak on the Bill. He said that he would speak about two things: the amount of money which is going toward servicing the debt; and the ravages of inflation on the elderly. There are some Canadians who can protect themselves to some degree from the ravages of inflation, but the elderly, who are on fixed incomes and below the poverty line in many cases, are not able to react as quickly. In some cases, they cannot react at all. It takes me back to the point which I just made: to develop a social policy of which we can all be proud, we must get our economic house in order. The only way to do that is for government to start placing a higher priority on economic matters than this Government has done.
Returning to the Bill, I have already stated that our Party supports the increase in the supplement. What else does the Bill do? The Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) has been pressing for changes to the War Veterans Allowance Act for a number of years. Other Members on our side have been pressing for changes as well, but he has been especially vocal on that issue. Some changes to the War Veterans Allowance
June 4, 1984

Act are included in the Bill. I would like to say to the Government, and to the Minister specifically, that in committee, we intend to examine the details not only with respect to those provisions but also the provisions which have been put forward by my colleague from Victoria.
I recall in 1977 debating changes to the Old Age Security Act with respect to immigrants. The Minister responsible for National Health and Welfare at that time is now Minister of Finance. At that time the Conservative Party raised the point that in future years the immigrant population would increase and have all the rights of citizens once they received their citizenship, but that they would always have difficulty with pensions. We asked at what stage would those immigrants have to be considered if the Government could not give their pensions proper adjustment. We asked at what stage-and the Minister used the words herself-would we have to look at social assistance or social welfare.
The provision which is before us today addresses, at least in part, the mistake that was made in 1977. I would like to say to the Minister that by putting the provision forward she is not doing something new, but rather in part correcting the mistake of her own Government which was made in 1977.
At the present time there is a one-year pay-back period for a person who applies for Old Age Security after the age of 65 which is being increased by the Bill. That is a provision which obviously we endorse. However, there is another provision which creates great concern. I am sure every Member of the House has had the experience of being visited by a senior citizen-and generally they are widows-between the ages of 60 and 65 who is neither eligible for Old Age Security nor for the spouse's allowance. In my experience those are the most difficult cases. These women have spent their working years in the home. They have probably given the greatest contribution to our country that anyone could, namely the mothering of their children and the raising of their familities. But they have no pension plan. They do not have skills the marketplace needs and therefore they cannot find work. If they do find work, very often because of the physical nature of the work they are not capable of doing it because of their age. If there is a huge gap in our pension system, it is in that area. I look forward to a very early opportunity, after the next election when we form the government, to correct that fallacy. I would have hoped that the Bill would have corrected it today. I would have given credit to the Government if it had seen that mistake, after the cajoling and pressuring that has come from the House and, more importantly, from many single people, especially women. It is an issue which must be corrected at the very first opportunity. It is unfortunate that the Bill does not afford us that opportunity.
The House is now in possession of an excellent report on pension reform which was presented by the Special Committee on Pension Reform. It is interesting to note that pension reform, at least in my judgment, must and will become one of the top priority items on the national agenda in the next few years. That will happen for a number of reasons. I have already mentioned some of those reasons which include the
Old Age Security Act
economic reasons. However, there are other reasons. For example, our demographic reality is changing as a country. I do not like the term "an aging population". Somehow I think it is inaccurate. But the fact remains that at the present time approximately 12 per cent of our population is over the age of 65. By the turn of the century it is estimated that we will be approaching the 20 per cent figure.
That being the case, for those of us who try to plan for the future, there will be a greater demand on our health care system, there will be a greater demand on housing services, and specifically, for our purpose today, there will be a greater demand on the pension system. We must get our economic house in order so that we can meet that developing reality.
It is also equally important that we put in provisions whereby people can become participants in pension plans which are self-contributory, company-contributory, or a combination thereof, in order that when they retire they are not only subject to Old Age Security and the guaranteed income supplement. I have no doubt that those two plans will keep Canadians, whether it is 1984 or 2004, in or below the poverty line level. That is reality. The history of pensions will dictate that.
Having said that, there are a number of provisions dealing with pension reform which I would have hoped the Minister would consider in the Bill. The Minister said recently that private pension plans must be overhauled and reformed. She had an opportunity to begin the legislative process in this Bill but, unfortunately, it was not done. There is absolutely no doubt, when we look at the demographic realities of Canada, that we must address those questions.
The Minister also pointed out that she was ready to sign agreements. She indicated that the last social security agreement which she signed was with Belgium. We now have, I believe, seven of those plans in place. However, I suggest we must put much more effort into getting an agreement with the United Kingdom.
I am aware of the argument that possibly the Government of the United Kingdom is not at the moment ready to move. However, there are many Canadians who have lived in Britain, who have paid into the British pension plan and who are now residents or citizens of Canada, who have had a portion of their British pension plan benefits frozen. We must get an agreement for those Canadians because they have paid into that plan. We have an obligation to those people to ensure they can receive the benefits for which they have paid. I suggest to the Minister even in the last days of the Government of which she is a member that she make that item a priority. I want to tell the Minister and Canadians who are unfortunately facing that dilemma that there is a full commitment on our part that when we become the government we will make that a top priority item.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to end with the obligations we have to Canada's seniors. I am always concerned, when legislation such as this is brought before us, the timing of

June 4, 1984
Old Age Security Act
it, that it could be seen not as pension reform but rather as a good or opportune political moment to give some emphasis to Canada's elderly. While we welcome this Bill, I believe the time is past when we should simply say: "Let us have some legislation. It is $25 today. It was $30 in the last election campaign, and we are going to get the elderly vote that way". In fact, Mr. Speaker, if one wanted to be absolutely cynical, one could say: "Let us create two openings, one for July, in case we want a summer election, and another one in December, in case we want a fall election. And we have both covered with $25".
I say through you, Mr. Speaker, let us not play games that way. The reason I say this is that I had an opportunity to speak to the eastern Manitoba seniors' council this last weekend. There were 130 senior citizens present from my riding who are representatives of some 28 senior citizens' clubs with some 1800 members. We talked about pension reform, among other topics, and it was interesting to note how quickly these senior citizens in Manitoba raised a concern about the move- and the Minister mentioned this-of the Minister of Social Development in the Province of Quebec. While it was not going to affect Manitoba, these citizens were concerned about what happens when we start making these changes or these adjustments. What is going to happen to their financial security? Are they vulnerable?
I believe the point which is so important to make is that these are Canadians who have contributed to our country and who are now in a position where they have made plans for the future based on the present pension system. Therefore, when I speak of pension reform, I believe what we should concentrate on is building on what we have. In other words, I am in favour of reform, not revolution. Let us reform the system but let us not create fear, as did the Quebec initiative, at least in the minds of some senior Canadians who obviously have looked at pensions very seriously and who take their economic reality on a day to day basis very seriously as well.
I would like to say in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that we have a long way to go on pension reform. In order to achieve that reform, we must have economic development and recovery. I want to say to Hon. Members of the House, and to Canadians, that our Party will support this legislation in a speedy manner in order that these moneys, which we believe these Canadians deserve, will be received before the end of this month.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my Party I want to assure the Minister as well that we want to see this measure passed by the House as quickly as possible.
I was curious about something which the Minister said at the conclusion of her remarks to the effect that following an election campaign the Government should speedily proceed in the area of pension reform. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that I have been hearing that ever since I came here in 1980. My research on that question has been going on much longer than that.
I have to say that I share the concerns expressed by the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), on behalf of himself
and his Party, that because of the parliamentary timetable which is left to us, there is a real danger that this Bill would not see the light of day in terms of enactment. The Government has allocated two days for this debate, I believe, today and possibly Wednesday or Thursday, I am advised. We would then see the Bill referred to committee.
What the committee does with the Bill, of course, is entirely up to that committee. However, it is conceivable that this measure would not come back into the House until after the Liberal leadership convention. Who knows what is going to happen then. We could be into an election and all kinds of things.
In light of that, Mr. Speaker, if it would be helpful to the Minister, I would be prepared on behalf of the New Democratic Party to make an offer to the Minister that she probably could not refuse. That would be to give consideration to all stages of this Bill today so that the measure could be enacted today. The Bill is not complicated. It is straightforward. The measures proposed in the Bill are recognized by every Hon. Member of this House as being of benefit to the individuals who will be the beneficiaries of it. So I repeat again, Mr. Speaker, that we in this Party would be prepared to follow precedents which have taken place in this House previously on measures which I do not believe to be as crucial or as important as this legislation, and deal with all the measures in this Bill through all stages in this sitting day. Therefore, at the end of this sitting day the seniors of this country would know that they would receive the $25 on July 1 and the other $25 in December as a fact rather than something they could only expect.

I have dealt with my first concern, Mr. Speaker. The other concern I have-I would welcome clarification from the Minister either during the course of this debate or during the lunch hour-is that the Minister said at the end of her remarks that this $50 increase over the six-month period would raise all seniors above the poverty level. There have been a number of organizations which have a tremendous degree of credibility in the country with respect to their research capabilities. They have come up with figures which are very similar to the figures I have. I want to read them because I think it is important that the House realize there are figures which dispute the Minister's figures. My figures show there will be a substantial number of seniors in the country who will still have an annual

income much below the poverty line. I welcome my figures being disputed if indeed the other figures can be substantiated.
For example, in St. John's Newfoundland, after all the increases have been passed on, my figures indicate that a single person would still have an income of $2,769 below the poverty level, and a married couple would be $961 below the poverty line. In Charlottetown it would be $1,520 for a single person and $702 for a couple. In Halifax, the single would be $2,550 and $523 for a couple. Saint John, New Brunswick, $2,769 for a single and $961 for a couple. In Montreal it would be $3,266 for a single and $1,627 for a couple. In Toronto it would be $2,560 and $369 respectively. In Winnipeg it would be $3,178 and $1,522. In Regina it would be $2,469 and $421. In Edmonton it is $2,126 and $653. In Vancouver a single person would still have an income of some $2,799 below the poverty level and for a couple it would be $431.
I believe our figures are as accurate as anyone else's, Mr. Speaker. As I said previously, I would welcome the Minister responding to those figures and perhaps giving us the figures she has so we can compare them. Then people across this country will know whether these changes are going to be of the assistance the Minister's Department feels they should be.
I appreciate that the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) has a rough row to hoe in Cabinet. Because of Cabinet solidarity, of course, I doubt very much whether she can express that opinion. However, I know from my own personal experience with other Cabinet Ministers that money for pensioners is not easy to pry out from the larger pie for a whole variety of reasons. Seniors know that very well because they made their presentations in a very eloquent and articulate manner to the task force on pension reform. However, there are some contradictions between what the Government says it wants to do regarding the GIS and what it is actually doing. As you know, Mr. Speaker, our Party is not what you would call a great supporter of the GIS. We would much rather see an expansion of the Canada Pension Plan and the public system than a GIS means test, or an increase across the board in the OAS. By the way, there is a large number of people out there who think that the $50 increase is in the OAS and not the GIS. Some people are going to be in for a rude awakening when they discover they are not going to get the $50 a month increase.
Lastly, Mr. Speaker, I want to refer to what the Department of Finance and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) did in the last Budget to persons collecting workmen's compensation pensions. The Government changed the rules so that those pensions are now included in the calculation of income for GIS purposes. The Minister wrote a letter to the chief executive officer of War Amputations of Canada. She said that to ignore income from sources such as workmen's compensation would result in inequitably higher benefits for pensioners who have such sources of income than for pensioners without such sources. She said the purpose of the GIS is to ensure that every
Old Age Security Act
pensioner is guaranteed the same basis level of income. I never thought, Mr. Speaker, that meant reducing another person's income in order to make sure that higher income earners are making the same as bottom earners. I would have thought a more honourable thing to do would be to raise people from the bottom up to the top.
The one thing the Government ignores is that there are definite additional costs associated with being disabled. The House of Commons Special Committee on the Disabled and the Handicapped made no less than 11 recommendations on that very question. We recognize that a person on a fixed income has associated additional expenses that an able-bodied person does not have. In all fairness to those individuals, the Government should have taken that into account. Certainly the Cabinet, in its response to that report, seemed to indicate that it fully understood that and would have some empathy for that argument. But what the Government did was to change the income tax system in order to chop away benefits from those individuals who were not otherwise affected in collecting the GIS.
I could say much, much more on this question. However, in the spirit of my previous remarks and my offer on behalf of the NDP to both the Government and the Official Opposition, I will not use up the entire time allocated to me. Rather than do that, I would ask the House for unanimous consent to move a motion to deal with all stages of Bill C-40 this day and refer the Bill to Committee of the Whole.

Mr. Speaker, the question of getting this Bill through the House as quickly as possible is one which this Party has been urging for some time. In fact, just a few days ago I initiated an Opposition debate on that very issue urging that the Bill come forward. I know the Minister appreciates that they are complex because it took her four or five months to prepare the Bill. Those matters have to be looked at and given-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I do feel that we are entering debate. It is quite apparent that there is no unanimous consent given by the House to change the motion at this time. Therefore, for continuing debate, the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor).

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on this Bill because I am very interested in a number of items in it. The $25 increase in July and November is certainly supported by all Members of the House. However, there are other things in the Bill which I think have to be considered. Quite frankly, I think they should be considered in committee unless the House Leaders can come to some other decision. I do not want to continue discussing the point of order, but I do not think the floor of the House is the place to discuss procedures of the House. That is why we have House Leaders. I guess that is enough said on that.
To begin with, I would like to deal with the specific matter of deductions for the purpose of arriving at the amount of money that we permit a person to secure the old age pension. I refer particularly to workmen's compensation. A question was asked the other day in the House with regard to a worker's compensation. I think the Minister had the wrong idea entirely of what partial permanent disability really means under the workmen's compensation Acts of the various provinces.
In no sense of the word is a PPD "income". When a man or woman is injured in industry, they go on regular compensation and secure two-thirds or three-quarters of their salaries for remuneration. That is income. They are unable to work and are paid this amount in order to continue living because the accident took place in industry. At the end of that time there is an assessment period. The work person is examined again to see if there is a partial permanent disability, a permanent partial disability or permanent total disability. It could be any of these. Permanent total disability would mean that perhaps both legs and both arms were gone or there was a very serious injury to the back which put a person in a wheelchair. That would be a total permanent disability.
When that occurs, surely we are not going to consider that as income. That is compensation because part of the body was left in the workplace. They were injured in the workplace through no fault of their own. They carry that loss throughout their lives. If that is to be considered income, the next step will be when a person like that obtains employment. A person who has lost both eyes, which would be almost total permanent disability, could not go to work because his income would be considered total income. Presently when a person employs someone who was completely blinded by employment, he is able to secure wages. It is recognized that that is compensation for the loss of the two eyes rather than payment for what he does afterward.
It is the same for a person who loses two legs or both arms. These people should not be penalized when they get to the age of 65 by suddenly making the compensation wages. That is completely contrary to compensation acts. That is completely contrary to what union people and others have fought for throughout the years. I do not like to see this even though it
June 4, 1984

may affect only a few. The principle which is being established is not sound. It is not at all sound to consider a permanent total disability or a permanent partial disability pension as income. It is not income. It is compensation for the loss of part of the body or sometimes practically all of the body. The industry is paying compensation because part of the body was left in the workplace. That should not be considered as income for Old Age Security or any portion of Old Age Security. Income for Old Age Security is a different thing entirely.
The Government did go so far as to say that pensions granted to veterans who left part of their bodies on the battlefield would not be considered as income. That is right. Veterans who have left part of their bodies on the battlefield should not have their pensions considered as income. It is not income at all. It is compensation or pension because part of their body was lost in fighting for the country. The principle is really the same. We grant one and refuse to grant the other.
I think this is because there is a misunderstanding of what compensation is. It is not payment of wages. This is particularly so with regard to a permanent partial disability pension or a permanent total disability pension. It is not wages; it is compensation because part of the body was left in the workplace. I think that should be corrected when this matter goes before committee.
I would briefly like to discuss another point in the Bill. That is the reduction in residence qualifications for the spouse's allowance. I support that particular item. It would reduce from 40 years to 10 years the residence requirement for a full spouse's allowance. This is a worth-while amendment that is overdue. When a pensioner with whom a person over the age of 60 lives passes away, then certainly the ten-year residence should be sufficient. However, I even question the need of the ten-year requirement.
Let me deal with another aspect of the spouse's allowance. There are cases where the wife of an old age pensioner is working and does not apply for the spouse's allowance. They may be able to get by on her wages and his pension and therefore they do not take advantage of applying for the spouse's allowance. However, when the old age pensioner passes away, the wife is left only with her wages which are not enough to live on. She still must pay the rent and all the other costs of the residence. The only difference is that now she only has to feed herself. When she applies for the spouse's allowance, she is refused because she did not apply while her husband was living. She is refused even though she is over 60 years old and her residency qualifications are sound.
I think that mistake should be corrected. A person should not be penalized because she tried to help the country by working when she could have quit working while her spouse was living and applied for the spouse's allowance. By not applying for that allowance and attempting to save the Government money, the wife is now unable to get the spouse's allowance. This case may not occur very often, but it affects some of our senior citizens who are now denied the spouse's
Old Age Security Act
allowance because they did not apply while their husbands were living. That principle is neither sound nor right.
I am in favour of the bilateral agreements. There are a number of my constituents who came from Belgium, Austria, Germany, Czechoslovakia and almost every European and Asian country. Since some of them have pensions coming from their homeland, it is a far better arrangement to have an agreement between the two countries so they do not have continually to contact their homelands. It takes weeks and sometimes months to get a reply from some countries, particularly those dominated by the U.S.S.R. Therefore, any bilateral agreement that is achievable can only help because it will assist our citizens to get a better pension.
Let me speak generally about the adequacy of pensions today. Certainly in the Province of Alberta, a pensioner who secures any portion of the GIS secures a portion of the Alberta assured income. Although I am unaware of the situation in other provinces, the residents of Alberta who receive a full GIS will secure the full Alberta assured income. This is probably true in other provinces and it is very helpful because the additional amount from provincial governments may, in many cases, bring people over the poverty line and remove the fear of what may happen tomorrow. I am in favour of anything we can do in that regard.
I am disturbed by the fact that when pensioners receive a pension of any type, it becomes virtually a fixed income. This might be acceptable if other costs remain fixed but the fact is that nothing remains fixed in our society. The cost of living, rents and taxes go up and while there is some indexing with regard to the total cost of living, it does not affect many items that are necessary for the livelihood of our people. Their pensions are not sufficient to replace worn out blankets or to make house repairs. While the pension may be sufficient to look after their everyday needs, other programs are necessary to meet these other costs. For example, if a pensioner is forced to move because his rent has suddenly gone up, it is difficult to meet the additional costs and any additional money that can be provided by other benefits would certainly be well worth while.
I support the program which the Alberta Government provides for widows over the age of 55. They are a group that have been left out of our country's social programs and such a program is of substantial help to them. Generally speaking, Canadian women between the ages of 50 and 65, unless they are on spouse's allowance, have nowhere to turn except welfare. Having worked all their lives, they should not end up on welfare. Most women at that age are unable to build up a Canada Pension because they have stayed at home to look after an invalid member of the family or an aging mother or father. When they are faced with no income they are told that the only alternative is to apply for welfare. That is not good enough in a country like Canada. We should be facing this problem and tackling it.
While there are some men faced with this dilemma, it is women in particular who cannot get back into the workforce when they reach that age because there is no place for them.

June 4, 1984
Old Age Security Act
Some of them find work scrubbing floors. I think it is unacceptable in this country that a woman who gets to the age of 50 or 60 must go out and scrub floors or do washing when her health is at stake. There are pitiful cases such as these in Canada, including in my riding where women are now existing, not living, on welfare. The very fact that they have to accept welfare is an affront to them. However, one must face this prospect when one is hungry and there are no other provisions.
Certainly it would help to lower the pension age somewhat, we must do something for these women between the ages of 50 and 65 even if it is on the basis of need. It is a blot on the social programs of Canada that they are left to depend solely on welfare. This should be corrected as soon as possible.
Although the $25 per month extra will help single pensioners, many of my constituents who are married pensioners are also having difficulty getting by. Their rents and other expenses have gone up. Their food costs are continually rising. They have asked why it is only single pensioners who are receiving the increase. They have difficulty accepting the explanation that two can live cheaper than one. In many cases the costs are the same because rent, tax, utilities, telephone and actual needs are not cheaper for two than for one. When only one pensioner receives an income, that pensioner must pay for everything. While there is no doubt that expenses are shared when there are two pensions, there is still a need among many of our married pensioners who barely meet the requirement for receiving the GIS.
The Hon. Minister mentioned a disturbing result when pensioners receive payments under these programs. They say they are now okay, that they have this part of the GIS and part of the assured income and can make a go of it. But the following year something happens to their income. They suddenly get a letter telling them to pay back certain sums of money to the Government. That is a nightmare to some of our pensioners who get these letters. Once they get the money, they spend it. They all have a need. As the Minister said, pensioners spend the money, they do not hoard it. They cannot. Few, if any, have bank accounts. Some try to put a little aside to look after funeral arrangements. You have to admire them for doing that. But not very many have bank accounts. It is a tragedy when they get letters saying that they have to pay back the money given to them inadvertently by the Government.
I think we should deal with that problem. I hope the committee will deal with it. It is a tragedy when people are suddenly told that the pension or the GIS they have received must now be paid back. The sums are not large, but they are large in relation to a pension.
This generation, as all generations, will be valued in history for the way we look after our senior citizens, particularly those in need, and for the way we look after our crippled, handicapped and retarded. I hope Canada will stand high when we get our social legislation put together in that we will not only
look after our aged, those over 65, but also those between the ages of 50 and 65 who need help, especially our women, our retarded and our crippled.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: There follows a ten-minute period for questions and comments. If there are no questions or comments, we will continue debate. The Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen).

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to speak to this measure which will increase the pension benefits for those receiving Old Age Security and the guaranteed income supplement. I have always felt that the first role of Government is to protect those who, through no fault of their own, are vulnerable in our society. It is for that reason that the spokesman for our Party, the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), has already indicated to the House that we plan to give speedy passage to the legislation. I hope the promise of speedy passage does not preclude an openness on the part of the Minister to accept changes by way of amendment at committee stage in order to improve protection for those who are vulnerable. By that I refer to amendments that would mean no further spending and which have nothing to do with tax revenues, but would simply improve the administration in such a way that the people who need to be protected will have that assurance.
Having said that, I accept the fact that we have probably not heard the last of this Bill. It is a strange perversity in this House that when we talk about measures passed in this Parliament that have become unpopular in the country, measures such as the National Energy Program, spokesmen on the other side in the Liberal Government say Parliament enacted this legislation. We hear them say that it was the will of Parliament that this should happen. But when it comes to measures like this one, it will not be Parliament which gave pensions or extended pensions; it will be the Liberal Government that did it. That is what we will be hearing in the weeks ahead.
As my colleague has indicated, it is not an accident of the calendar that benefits are staged to July and December so that if perchance we should be on the election trail in July and August or in October and November, members of the Liberal Party will be able to say, not in the high road of parliamentary language that Parliament enacted it, or that it was the wish of Parliament that pensioners get these extra benefits. No, by then we will revert to the former language. In other words, it will be the Liberal Government that gave these benefits.
We should not be deluded into thinking that we are talking about pension reform. We are talking about a supplement to what is already there. It is not in any way improving the benefits except to catch up with some of the inflationary pressures people on pension incomes have been facing. To some degree those who are vulnerable are made more vulnerable by what we are doing today. As we know, the GIS has created its own kind of dependency. Those who are vulnerable because they have to depend on all government pension plans are made more so by this Bill. It is because of the vicissitudes
June 4, 1984

of government and government services that they become increasingly vulnerable. I am talking about such things as the mail service, computer breakdowns, the change of address that has to be worked through the system, the increase in inflation which is beyond the technocracy of government or the control of the pensioner
Or the annual income report.

Or the annual income report. The fact is that adjustments are made always the quarter after the inflation increase or the cost of living increase. Then as my colleague mentioned, the exchange rates between the United Kingdom and Canada are another example. Because the pound sterling has fallen in relation to the Canadian dollar, it means a reduction in the pension amount for those pensionable by the United Kingdom. Those kinds of vicissitudes make the vulnerable even more so. Those of us who spend time in our constituency offices know the pressure that rests on people who depend upon government pensions and government services to deliver them.
If we are going to talk about pension reform, we must talk about ways to diversify pension income so that pensioners will not be so dependent upon only one source. We think to diversify income is a very clever method when it comes to business. What about farming businesses? When a farmer can, he will diversify his income through the crops that he plants. Business will diversify its investment as much as possible in order to make sure that when there are down years in one area, there is income from another.
Why should we not be able to diversify income through pensions by creating a tax structure in such a way that those who are pensionable should be able to look forward to a variety of sources for their pension and not be vulnerable because of the vicissitudes of government pension schemes? It seems to me that if we want to talk about pension reform, we ought to talk about diversifying rather than pyramiding pension sources.
There is something ominous and pernicious about this Bill. It not only gives, but it also takes away. I refer now to the workmen's compensation provisions within this legislation. The Minister in her speech gave all her attention to how the Government was lifting up all of the pensioners. In her letter to the gentleman in charge of the war amputees of Canada she gives her attention to how she is planning to take away. In her public statements she talks about how she wants to lift up the pensioners, but in her private letters it is how she is pressing them down. The perversity of this Government is that public attention will be on pension increases and the public who hears about it will be happy. The individual pensioners across the country who are vulnerable by way of workmen's compensation pensions will be pushed down and we will not hear about those, Sir. That is the politics of this legislation.

SUMMER CANADA STUDENT EMPLOYMENT PROGRAM-CALL FOR ADDITIONAL FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to impress upon the House the great need for additional funds for the Summer Canada Student Employment Program. The need for an expanded program is even more pronounced in areas of high unemployment like Newfoundland where summer jobs do not exist, generally speaking, in private enterprise, or in government Departments which are practically non-existent.

subtopic: USE OF HAWAIIAN ISLAND AS PRACTICE TARGET-DEMAND FOR CESSATION
USE OF HAWAIIAN ISLAND AS PRACTICE TARGET-DEMAND FOR CESSATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for a number of years the Canadian Navy had used the Hawaiian Island of Kahoolawe for shelling exercises. For a thousand years this island has been considered sacred to Hawaiian people. Yet from 1941 until 1979 its use for religious and cultural purposes was banned by the United States Navy.
In 1981 the entire island was added to the U.S. National Register of Historic Places because of its invaluable historic significance. At this very moment the Canadian Navy is again participating in exercises which include shelling this island,
exercises that pose an immediate threat to some of the archaeological sites, despite petitions from thousands of Hawaiians, despite resolutions from the State Legislature and municipal governments, in opposition to the shelling, and despite the fact that the navies of Japan, Australia and New Zealand have ceased their participation in shelling. To these entreaties the Canadian Government has shown an amazing insensitivity.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), two Ministers of National Defence and various government and military officials have dismissed out of hand Hawaiian concerns and their requests that Canada respect their cultural and religious heritage by withdrawing from the shelling exercises.
I call upon the Canadian Government to cease immediately any participation in any shelling of this region which is very important to Hawaiian people.

Mr. Speaker, June 6 marks the fortieth anniversary of the Allied D-Day offensive in Normandy which led to the liberation of Europe from Nazi occupation.
Operation Overlord was a great achievement. Five divisions reached the Normandy shores by sea, and three more by air. Seven thousand ships landed at the heavily fortified shoreline, in secrecy. Canadians will remember with pride the courageous efforts of our soldiers on Juno Beach. Canadian casualties numbered 946. The Queen's Own Rifles suffered the most, losing 143, The Winnipeg Rifles lost 128, and the North Shore Regiment had 125 casualties.
On Wednesday we will celebrate the victory, but let us not forget the dead who paid for their success in blood that we might remain free. Ten thousand Allied soldiers lost their lives in a battle which has become, as Time magazine put it, "an almost unconscious reply to the pacifist view of war".
If there ever was a just war in our history, it was the one in Europe 40 years ago. Every Canadian is aware of the philosophy of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) toward that war. Hopefully our veterans will feel pride as he represents Canada in Normandy in one of his final, official, international functions as head of the Government.
May the fallen Canadians of Juno Beach rest in peace.

subtopic: MEDICAL EXPENSES OF DISABILITY ALLOWANCE RECIPIENTS

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subtopic: MEDICAL EXPENSES OF DISABILITY ALLOWANCE RECIPIENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we hear a great deal these days about the adequacy of our social programs, but there are still those who fall between the various social safety nets. One such group com-
June 4, 1984

prises those under the age of 65 who suffer from debilitating diseases and have to pay an exorbitant amount of their income for drugs and medication. Because they are under 65, disability benefits from the Canada Pension Plan do not include the cost of drugs.
Let me cite the case of a man in my own constituency who is suffering from Parkinson's disease. He is 52 years of age, is married, and has two teenage children to support. Out of his meagre disability allowance he must pay S400 a month for medication to keep his illness under control. That is the bleak financial outlook for him and his family, month after month, year after year.
I am sure that the situation of this man is not unique. There must be many disability pension recipients under the age of 65 who desperately need assistance with their drug costs. While the matter is in part a provincial responsibility, nevertheless the federal Government surely has some obligation to do its part. I would therefore urge the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) to consult with her provincial colleagues with a view to taking early action on this critical issue.

subtopic: INCLUSION OF DISABILITY BENEFITS IN CALCULATION OF INCOME

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Hudecki (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: INCLUSION OF DISABILITY BENEFITS IN CALCULATION OF INCOME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, until 1982 workmen's compensation payments were not included in net income for income tax purposes. The November, 1981, Budget of the federal Government brought about a change such that all social assistance payments, whether made on the basis of a means, need, or income test, would be treated as net income and deducted when calculating taxable income. As a result, workmen's compensation payments are now included in the items to be treated as income when calculating net income, and deducted when calculating taxable income. The Old Age Security Act was amended to reflect this inclusion of workmen's compensation benefits in determining eligibility for GIS payments, as were other types of disability income payments.
1 am concerned that workers' compensation payments should not be included in net income for income tax purposes but, rather, that these funds should be used to help defray some of the additional expenses and suffering encountered by those who have been injured or disabled in the workplace. I therefore urge the Government to review its current policy regarding inclusion of Workmen's Compensation Board payments in the calculation of eligibility for GIS payments.

subtopic: PROPOSED REPLACEMENT OF DEFINITION OF HATE LITERATURE
PROPOSED REPLACEMENT OF DEFINITION OF HATE LITERATURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hate literature is appearing all too frequently across Canada and is hardly a victimless product. Indeed, it is a malignant growth on the banner of freedom of expression, and the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) has quite rightly called for the removal of two of the larger loopholes in the existing hate literature provision of the Criminal Code. That the existing Section is toothless is shown by the fact that there have been only four prosecutions under that Section in 14 years and that the one conviction was overturned on appeal.
As a former Crown and defence attorney, I believe that one major problem is the definition of hate literature in the Code,

June 4, 1984
Oral Questions
and I would propose the following replacement for the present definition:
Hate literature is defined as any printed or written material or communication which promotes hatred of, or violence toward, any grouping of persons on the basis of colour, religion, language or place of origin.
Two other legislative remedies would also be helpful, and these were proposed in Toronto over the weekend at my Party's conference on multiculturalism. One such remedy is that the Criminal Code should be amended to allow a court, upon conviction, to increase the sentence if it finds that a crime was motivated by racism. Second, the post office regulations should be amended to prevent people from sending hate literature through the mails. The inadequacy of the postal situation is well shown by the fact that Ernst Zundel lost his mail privileges but they were returned on appeal.
