The House resumed consideration of the motion of Miss Begin that Bill C-40, an Act to amend the Old Age Security Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, when we recessed for lunch I had been in the process of making what I think are two important points respecting amendments to the pension plans of Canada. The first concerns people who are vulnerable. They are the ones who as their total income upon retirement have the Old Age Security pension and the guaranteed income supplement. They are very unfortunate because they have to depend also upon government services. When those services break down, they are affected.
It would be a matter of pension reform if in the process the Government introduced the kind of tax system that would allow pensioners to diversify their retirement income. What about putting in the kind of tax amendments which would allow people to save during their lifetime and invest the money in such a way that when they do retire they would have various sources of income, instead of having to depend solely upon the Government OAS and other forms of pension.
My second point concerns workmen's compensation pensions. During the Minister's statement in the House, she was giving the general public the impression that all of these amendments deal with improving the position of pensioners, making them all feel better because they will be doing better under the pension system. That camouflages and disguises a section of this Bill that is really not to the benefit of pensioners, specifically those who are on disability pensions from workmen's compensation boards.
I know it is politically attractive to put the best face on things and make measures look as though everybody will benefit from them. What the Minister has done today is to let Canadians believe that everybody will be benefiting from this legislation. Meanwhile those people receiving income from workmen's compensation boards individually scattered across a Canada will lose income in relation to other pensioners.
I was glad to hear during statements made today support from the Hon. Member for Hamilton West (Mr. Hudecki), together with the applause given to his statement by the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mrs. Appolloni). There are members of the Government who are just as concerned as members of the Opposition about this provision. People who are receiving their income from workmen's compensation boards should not be jeopardized because of this particular amendment which the Government has introduced.
The Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young) mentioned a letter which the Minister sent to the War Amputees Association. Let me quote from one part of this letter. The Minister wrote:
To ignore income from sources such as Workmen's Compensation would result in inequitably, higher benefits for pensioners who have those sources of income than for pensioners without such sources.
That is the level of fairness the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) addresses and that is unfortunate. I suppose it is politically expedient to handle the matter that way.
My final point deals with the administration of the system. There are a number of amendments in this Bill which deal with the administration. I know the Minister was sincere in her comments during debate when she said that she wants to improve the administration of the pension scheme and make sure that the mechanisms in government do not create a built-in unfairness for pensioners, that there will be provisions in the administration of the pension system that will make it operate more fairly for all pensioners. I do not minimize the Minister's willingness to do this, her desire to improve things or her honesty in the statements that she has made today. I simply say they will not work because they are outside of her department.
I think all Members realize that, while we are passing provisions today under the jurisdiction of the Minister of National Health and Welfare and her administration, it is actually the Department of Supply and Services which does the work. They send out the cheques, they make the decisions, and when there are critical decisions affecting the pensions of senior citizens, they are not made as a rule by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. They are not necessarily made by officials in her Ministry. They are frequently made by members of the administration of the Department of Supply and Services.
I have a case in point and I will probably take the balance of the time allocated to me to illustrate the point I am trying to make. The case to which I should like to refer is that of a pensioner in my constituency whose husband had worked for the Government in the armed forces, in the post office and possibly in other government departments for most of his life. The couple had been married for 37.5 years at which point they were legally separated. In negotiating a legal separation the husband agreed that, upon his decease, his wife would receive all the death benefits. It was properly arranged in the lawyer's office and it was an amicable separation. Unfortunately the husband was an alcoholic, yet he realized he had an obligation to his wife. He wanted to look after her even though he was not living with her any longer.
Within a few months thereafter, having moved away and living in a different part of Canada, he signed a new agreement which denied to his spouse all death benefits. I realize the Bill we are discussing today deals with pensions, not with death benefits. In terms of a precise parallel it is not there except in the administration. I want Government Members to
June 4, 1984

understand that we are talking about the administration of these systems through the Department of Supply and Services.
There followed a nightmare of trying to negotiate some sense of justice. Indeed, the newly-named beneficiary was willing to waive her benefits and so announced to the Department of Supply and Services. She requested a form so that she could waive the death benefits. It so happened that the spouse was also the executrix of the will.
I should like to point out some startling facts. First, the Department of Supply and Services never had the courtesy of notifying the executrix of the change in beneficiary. Furthermore, departmental officials never offered an apology, never said that it was negotiable, nor told the executrix that the new beneficiary was willing to waive her benefits. I would like to point out what happened in the negotiations. The change in beneficiary was made six months after the signing of the separation agreement.
I see Mr. Speaker indicating that my time is almost up. I was told that I had 12 minutes remaining after the luncheon break and I do not think I have spoken for 10 of them. In any event, six months after the separation agreement was signed, the man was in the last days of his life; he was an alcoholic. There was no guarantee established that the new beneficiary had received that new status legally. Was he under the influence of alcohol? Had he already deteriorated in his health to the point that he did not know what he was doing? There was no attempt on the part of the Department to establish the legitimacy of that change in beneficiary.
Since my time is coming to an end, I underscore for the Government that earlier in the day I said we could not pass all stages today because there were some amendments which ought to be made that did not concern money; they concern the protection of the spouse under the administration of the Department of Supply and Services. When officials in that Department are engaged in nothing more than protecting their own backsides, in following precise regulations of the Department rather than looking after pensioners and their benefits, we need some very close scrutiny of the regulations. When a change in beneficiary can be so loosely worded as to deny a spouse who had been married for 37.5 years death benefits which were rightly hers, we need to tighten up the Bill so that there is justice for widows and spouses who would otherwise be denied benefits which ought to be accruing to them as a result of this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, in the nature of comments more than questions, I should like to refer to the Hon. Member's reference to myself as having applauded the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hudecki) today when he made a statement pursuant to Standing Order 21 about the fact that workmen's compensation payments are now included and therefore cause a deduction in the pension. I regret that very much indeed. Now that I am on the point of leaving, I can say that it was one of the few
Old Age Security Act
regressive steps ever taken by the Liberal Party. I believe compensation for disability should be ex gratia. It is society's only way to say thank you to veterans of war or victims of horrendous labour accidents. We should say thank you. We should not deduct money from them in any way.
Having said that, I challenge the Hon. Member in terms of another deduction from people who need the money most. We are talking about needy senior citizens to whom I made reference today during Question Period. My question was ably answered by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence. As a Conservative Member, the Hon. Member will know that most provincial governments in Canada are Conservative. If they profess humanity, every time the federal Government, usually a Liberal Government, gives badly needed money to the poorest people of Canada, why do provincial governments consistently take back what we try to give so that those who live in subsidized housing will have their rents geared to income? Here again we must define what is income. It is one of the most horrendous acts perpetrated by provincial governments. The fact is that when we give the $25 increase, the provincial governments will probably take most of it back for rents.
Another point I should like to make was referred to by the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp). In his speech he referred to the fact that he and some of his colleagues had long advocated help for immigrant people. Many of the immigrant people who both of us know are generally very old and came to Canada when they were already quite elderly. Because of their age or because of other reasons, they were unable to learn either English or French, the two official languages. In her speech this morning the Minister referred to many of these immigrants who constantly lose out on some of the programs being offered to them.
I urge the Minister and all those who may be listening today that when we propose some kind of relief for immigrant people, we tell them in a way they understand. In this case I am speaking about talking to them in their own language. Perhaps the advertising of these benefits should be done mainly through the so-called ethnic press. We have to reach them. In my own small way I have reached my constituents who speak Italian because I happen to know that language. However many of my constituents speak only Polish, Ukrainian, Greek or whatever and I cannot reach them. Therefore it is the Government's job to reach them in the language they understand. They need to know. It is to their benefit.

Mr. Speaker, certainly I will respond to the Hon. Member's remarks which related to me. She mentioned that provincial governments tend to siphon the moneys transferred to them. I am not sure that is always the case. However, I urge the Minister to use her powers in negotiating with the provinces to ensure that the people out there receive the full benefit of this increase. It is her obligation to do that between now and when the time of the Government runs out. The Minister of Health has an obligation to make sure that the people receive all of the benefits of this legislation.

June 4, 1984
Old Age Security Act
I would add to that that in the Province of British Columbia the provincial government tops up incomes over and above the OAS and the GIS. The Province of British Columbia has provision for a GAIN supplement, or a guaranteed annual income supplement, for those who are in need. The provincial Government of British Columbia and I suspect the provincial governments of other provinces are topping up the incomes of those who are already receiving OAS and GIS.
Third, the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mrs. Appolloni) mentioned the need for providing services in the language of the immigrants. I would agree that immigrants should not be denied any kind of help that they could possibly get. For example, I know that the father of the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) was once a translator in the courts. He translated for those who spoke only Russian or German and he provided that service through the years without any kind of government legislation obligating him to do so. The courts were generous and open-minded and they provided that service. Many of us in this House who speak more than one language do that in our riding offices all the time. We translate for those who speak German-the best language of all-or for those who speak other languages, and we do that constantly. I agree that we must accommodate those who do not speak either of the two official languages of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be taking part in this debate today and indeed to be addressing myself to this Bill which on other occasions I have urged the Government to bring before the House just as quickly as possible.
When I was looking at the Bill, I thought of the number of occasions over the past few years on which I have spoken of the need for pension reform. I began to go back through my own files and look at some of the most recent speeches that I made on this subject. Hardly a week has passed in the last two or three years during which I have not in some forum, either here in the House of Commons, before organizations across the country or on radio and television broadcasts, dealt with the subject of pension reform.
I have pointed out time and time again the pressing and urgent need for pension reform. In fact, as I look at this particular Bill and consider the issue, I would say that there is probably no other issue that has taken so much of my time, and I would say rightly so, in the last number of years. That is one of the reasons I am pleased to see this Bill finally come before the House.
While the Bill does not address the issue in any major way, it does deal with one of the components of the issue. It is a partial solution to what I think is the overriding social issue of our time. I went through the Bill and paid a great deal of attention to what the Minister said about it this morning. As
well, I listened with great care to other speakers and to the spokesperson for the Conservative Party, the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), who followed the Minister in the course of debate. At that time he gave the House the assurance that, as far as this Party was concerned, there would be speedy passage of the Bill. There should be no concern or doubt about that whatsoever.
Of course, there is one thing that we do wish to make very clear. There are items that are dealt with in this Bill that have not been mentioned previously. I am referring to some of the changes to the Act relating to spouses and some of the regulations with regard to pension adjustments that will be made for those who have emigrated to this country in recent years. Those are things which we will need to look at in some detail in committee, at least for a period of time, so that we do not make the mistake we made before of putting through legislation that we must subsequently correct. That has already happened two or three times with regard to various pension measures that needed changes. That happened in 1977 when we changed pensions for immigrants.
The House made mistakes and the Government made mistakes when it introduced the concept of a spouse's allowance. When the Conservative Government was in office in 1979, it took a step to correct at least one of the inequities with regard to the spouse's allowance that needed to be corrected. We were required to readdress legislation that had already been passed. I think it is very important that we take the limited time that will be necessary to look at this Bill in committee in order to ensure that we do not once again make mistakes that will create further inequities with regard to pensions across the country.
The Minister mentioned a couple of other things today to which I wish to allude. She herself mentioned the fact that single elderly persons require more than half the income of married elderly couples in order to get by; that when one spouse dies, the income of the remaining spouse should not be cut in half because the rent, taxes, transportation costs and heating costs are not automatically cut in half. I point that out because the Minister herself raised the matter.
It was on that basis that the parliamentary task force on pension reform brought in a proposal to increase the guaranteed income supplement for single elderly persons to at least two-thirds of the income of married elderly couples. We thought that that would be fair and even more fair than proposals that are now before us. The Government did not see fit to accept that recommendation. I think that recommendation would have done a great deal to alleviate the poverty of those most in need. They would have been the ones who would have been helped most. We in the all-Party Special Committee on Pension Reform felt that that would be the proper way to go.
The Minister has chosen to introduce an amendment which will increase the guaranteed income supplement for single elderly persons by $25 on July 1 and $25 on December 1. Certainly that is better than nothing. However, contrary to what the Minister said this morning, it does not bring the
June 4, 1984

incomes of all of those single persons who are over the age of 65 above the poverty line. She said that it would but it will not. In my own community of Kingston, for example, a city of moderate size, the incomes of single elderly persons will still fall $1,700 short of the poverty line even after these two increases are implemented.
We should try to put the increase in the incomes of elderly persons in proper perspective. This increase will allow the income of a single person over the age of 65 to become $20 a day. When one thinks of the expenditures that must come from that $20, one realizes that we are not talking about any degree of affluence. It is far from affluence. Out of that $20 a day must come money for food, transportation, taxes, health care and a good many other things. When those things are paid for, very little is left over for those things which I like to call things of the soul: concerts, plays and all such other things that many people over the age of 65 must deny themselves.
The Minister said this morning that the Government brought in the increase as soon as the economy permitted it. I take some exception to that. I would like to know why it took so long to find out that the economy permitted it. When I look at some of the Minister's earlier statements I find, for example, that in March of 1981 she said:
We have often repeated the commitment of this Government to bring all the senior citizens who now receive the supplement over the poverty line.
Two years later, in March, 1983, the Minister repeated her claim and qualified it somewhat. She said:
The cost of bringing the single pensioners over the poverty line... has been approved by the Government as their first social spending-whenever we can afford it.
June, 1984, is obviously when the Government thinks the first social spending should take place. However, the economy permitted in the last two years that $2.1 billion be given to Canadair; it permitted almost $1 billion for de Havilland; it permitted $34 million for Maislin; and it permitted the executives of Crown corporations such as CDIC and de Havilland to receive large bonuses. It permitted all of these things. The economy could afford all of those, but it could not afford the $450 million for increases to the guaranteed income supplement until just before an election. That is interesting. Nevertheless, having said this, there is no question that we want to see the Bill being given speedy passage.
The guaranteed income supplement goes to some 700,000 Canadians, either in part or in full. I would like to take a look at those 700,000 people. When we examine who they are and when we talk about who are the recipients, we look at the question of Canada's elderly poor. When we do that, we can determine very easily who it is we are really talking about. Eighty per cent of the single elderly today who live below the poverty line are women. Four out of every five of the people living below the poverty line in their retirement years-their so-called golden years-are women. Those women did not ask to be put in that position. They contributed throughout their lifetimes to build this country. Today they find themselves in
Old Age Security Act
very, very straightened circumstances. Eighty per cent of the elderly poor in Canada today are women. Eighty per cent of the elderly poor in Canada tomorrow will be women, unless we do more than provide band-aid solutions by coming along after the fact to address the problems of those over the age of 65. This is where I take the greatest exception to the present legislation: it does not address the issue of pension reform.
Pension reform cannot be undertaken after the age of 65. It must be addressed while people are still below that age-in their earning years; in their contributing years-from the point of view of being part of the labour force. We cannot wait until those people reach the age of 65 to carry out pension reform. The reason that I dwell on this and have dwelled on it increasingly over the years, is that I and my Party consider pension reform to be one of the major pillars in guaranteeing economic equality to women in this country.
Why do I put this emphasis on how important it is to the women of the country that something be done about it? Quite frankly, unless something substantial is done in the way of pension reform before people get to the age of 65, we will see many more women living below the poverty line 10, 20 and 30 years in the future. Let me say why. There are still-and people often try to dismiss this-almost three million people who work full-time in the home. The great majority of them are women. They are people who, at the present time, do not have access to pension plans in their own right. Many of them are in a marriage contract which could quite conceivably dissolve before they reach the age of 65. What will they have in their own right to allow them to carry on pension payments in the future? If we were to go beyond that and look at others who do not have adequate retirement income, we could focus in on the five million people who are in the paid labour force today, who have no supplemental benefits or access to a pension plan beyond the Canada Pension Plan. They are not in a defined benefit plan and they have no company plan. They have, perhaps, very little money to put into a retirement savings plan. There are five million such people in Canada today. The majority of them, once again, are women. These are people whose average income is probably between $12,000 and $25,000 a year. They could, with proper fiscal encouragement and tax credits, be encouraged to begin to look to their own retirement future. However, at the present time, many of them find it impossible to do so.
It is substantial pension reform which we really need to turn the situation around and to make it possible for older people to face their retirement years with some sense of dignity and self-worth.
I would like to quote from a speech which I gave two years ago this month in Toronto. I said to the group at that time:
Let us look at the situation of our elderly poor today, and call it what it is, a national disgrace.
These elderly are treated worse than many whom we convict and condemn for crimes of theft and violence. Yet what did they do wrong? Do they ask to grow old? To outlive friends and relative? To be widowed or divorced? To be denied gainful work by age or inexperience or health? To be written off and forgotten? To live in small and dingy rooms, seldom eating a nourishing and balanced meal?

June 4, 1984
Old Age Security Act
Sometimes, when I have spoken of these elderly Canadians, most of them women, I have been reminded of the millions around the world far worse off, caught in wars, and in famine. And it is true, very few of our elderly, even those hundreds of thousands of women over 65 who live below the poverty line, actually die from starvation or pestilence. None from war or political terrorism. Ours is a benign, not a wilful neglect.
It is that, above all, which is so shameful about our present pension system and its treatment of the Canadian woman.
I made this speech two years ago. I went on to say:
There was no deliberate intention to bring about the situation as it exists today. It just happened. It happened because we were not sufficiently alert. We weren't interested enough. We didn't know.
No one can pretend to have all the answers to such an immense problem and the causes behind it. But I do know that if we are now to rebuild our pension system we must do so as comprehensively as possible. We must not do it by half measure. We must not overlook, underestimate, or ignore any part of our society. Especially women.
That is what I have been saying, Sir, for the last two, three and four years on this subject.
I am pleased to see this Bill come before us today. Yes, I am pleased to see the measures which are incorporated. However,
I do point out to you, Sir, that it is just a very timid step. It does not begin to address the major problem of pension reform. We here in this House must feel the responsibility to address this problem. We must take it on, because if we do not, Sir, those people who will be in the senior citizen bracket 10, 20 and 30 years down the road will point to us, and rightly so, and say, "When you had the opportunity for action, you failed to take it. You failed us and, particularly, you failed the women of Canada". That kind of condemnation, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to receive, and I will do everything possible to make sure that that does not happen. That is why I say that this Bill does not go nearly far enough. We must have much more than this legislation in the way of pension reform.

speakeroldname: Mr. Russell MacLellan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to be able to enter into the debate on the Bill before us this afternoon. I have listened to the various speakers who have spoken prior to myself and what concerns me the most is the little regard which Hon. Members opposite have for the actual advantages and benefits of the Bill which is before us today. I do agree with the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) and other Hon. Members, that perhaps it would be nice if more could be done in this Bill, or in general, for our senior citizens. I believe that is true. I do not believe there is an Hon. Member in this House who would disagree with that philosophy. I agree with the statement that more should be done for people over the age of 65 and, in particular, women in need. And I agree, as the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands points out, that women do form the majority of those in need over the age of 65. I
disagree, however, with the Hon. Members opposite for the little regard they hold for this Bill. I believe this Bill is a very significant step forward and I will tell you why, Mr. Speaker.
The Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands and other Hon. Members have suggested that this Bill should contain more benefits, that it should contain more changes, that perhaps it could be meatier, more in respect of the whole question of pension reform. At the same time Hon. Members opposite have criticized the Government for not bringing the Bill forward earlier, in spite of the fact that the provisions which are in the Bill today were mentioned in the Budget of February 15. The Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands herself, on an Opposition Day or May 10, criticized the Government for not bringing forward these amendments. In spite of the fact that she knew that the first $25 increase would take effect on July 1, she was still pressing the Government to do something. We are now doing something. We have this Bill before us today.
Why did it take you so long?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
The New Democratic Party moved a motion that all stages of this Bill be dealt with today. We on this side agreed to that, but members of the Progressive Conservative Party said that they needed more time to study certain aspects of the legislation. If members of the Progressive Conservative Party are sincere in their intention to study positively and quickly all aspects of this Bill, then that point of view is acceptable to us. I do hope they are sincere when they say they do not wish to prolong debate on this Bill and want it to come into effect as soon as possible. It is very important that this Bill go to committee. I hope that the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), who is the health critic for his Party, would agree that, if there are amendments or questions he would like to bring forward in committee, those questions will be dealt with as quickly as possible, not to shorten the time spent on it, but so as not to delay the meetings in committee so that this Bill can receive swift passage.
The Hon. Member for Provencher has mentioned, and I feel rightly so, that there are two Bills before the committee at the present time, Bill C-221, which deals with the therapeutic use of heroin, and Bill C-5 dealing with the question of radiation. He is a member of the steering committee and knows that the dates for hearings on these Bills were agreed to by all members of all Parties in this House. If he wishes to change the order of the hearings before the standing committee and bring Bill C-40 before the committee prior to the other Bills, I will support him in that. However, to say that because these Bills are before the committee the Government is not sincere in dealing with the provisions of this Bill I feel is totally false and really very misleading. I would hope that he will state his preferences in this regard.
The Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands is concerned about the welfare of women in this country and, I feel rightly so. However, I would like to say, in all fairness to the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands, that she does not have a corner on this concern for women and for the pension-
June 4, 1984

ers in this country. We listened to the comments of the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mrs. Appolloni) stating her concern that the provinces pass along to the pensioners in their provinces the benefits of the increases in the guaranteed income supplement, that they not do what they have done in the past and reduce the welfare payments correspondingly. When we increase our GIS payments on July 1, they should not reduce their payments to those very same people by the same amount of $25. I believe it is the duty of all Members of this House of Commons to present to their respective provinces their concern that the provinces pass along the benefit of this GIS increase to the people in those particular provinces. I do not doubt that that will be the case. However, I want to emphasize the importance of Members of Parliament taking a stand on this very important question.
I would like to mention also that when we are talking about women and poverty, Mr. Speaker, we are not only talking about women over the age of 65. The Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands knows, as we all know, that there is a problem in other areas. The Hon. Member has said that the problem of income for pensioners is probably the most serious social question facing this country today. I do not disagree that it is a serious question. However, there are other serious questions.
I said pension reform.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Pension reform is one of the most serious questions, that is true. I still disagree with the Hon. Member but I appreciate her clarification. There are other social questions of very great importance to our country at the present time which involve women in their role as single parents, as mothers and wives. There are unemployed women and men without jobs who, along with their children, are living below the poverty line. There is the problem of our young people who have been out of college perhaps for two or three years who have not yet been able to get that first job. Their problem will be compounded as they go through life because, through no fault of their own, they are picking up the stigma of being unemployed. And when jobs do become available, as they will, they will see those jobs offered to those who have just graduated from high school or university because, supposedly, these new graduates have not been unemployed, have not come in contact with what is seen in the minds of some employees as the stigma of unemployment. These are the social problems we face and they must be addressed.
Bill C-40 is an important step for pensioners. Hon. Members opposite say that the Bill should contain more, and at the same time they say we must get it passed as soon as possible. They know that if clauses are added, the Bill will, in their opinion, become more contentious, and the more they will want to debate it, the more they will pick holes in it in committee. I did not arrive here yesterday, Mr. Speaker. I have been here for five years and I have been watching Members opposite. I know the way they work.
Old Age Security Act
This morning the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) said that 55 per cent of Canadian workers do not have pensions. Imagine if we tried to put forward in this Bill an ever so slight requirement for mandating of pensions in the private sector. Imagine the outcry from Members opposite. Imagine how long it would take to deal with this Bill. We want to get these provisions to the people in need, the pensioners, as soon as possible. In order to do that, we have to present a realistic Bill which will be passed, and that is what the Government has done. It does not provide all the answers; no one says it does. But it does provide answers to some very serious problems. We hope Members' opposite realize that and deal with it constructively. I recommend that they do not posture on this very important issue.
It was mentioned by the Hon. Member for York South-Weston that there are relatively new elderly citizens in our country who are not aware of these benefits. This Bill deals with this question in that it would make payments to pensioners retroactive for five years, whereas it is one year at present. This is very significant. Mind you, it may only affect 50 people a year, but it shows the concern of the Minister and of the Government for the well-being of even 50 people when provisions such as this are included in the Bill. In addition, the Minister has agreed to advertise these benefits in the ethnic press so that people of various ethnic origins can read in their own language about the benefits now available to them. Of course, we will then have allegations from the Opposition that the Liberals are trying to advertise what they are doing for the people of Canada. It will not be termed as a benefit to the people concerned; it will be termed as advertising for the Liberal Government. How are you supposed to do what the Opposition asks without being open to unfair allegations such as that?
The question of British pensioners, Mr. Speaker, is of concern to the Opposition as it is to the Minister. Pressure has been put on the British Government. The Minister is now considering following up this question as far as she possibly can.
About time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I think the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands knows very well how sincere the Minister is on this question. As Members opposite know, economic dossiers associated with questions of foreign countries are dealt with through the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen). The Minister is prepared to bring this question into the economic dossiers through the Department of External Affairs in the hope that it can be resolved. Once again this indicates the consideration the Minister is giving to these very important questions.
The Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands talked about the inability of people over the age of 65 to attend concerts and listen to music and so on. She knows there are areas in this country where concerts are not available except through radio and television. That underlines once again the fact that social issues must be looked at through the perspec-
4336

June 4, 1984
Old Age Security Act
tive of need and that all questions of social need in this country must be considered.
She also mentioned that we are bringing this Bill forward before a federal election. This issue was mentioned in the Budget of February 15. We all know what the polls were like then. They certainly were not as favourable to the governing Party as they are at the present time. Whoever assumed on February 15 that there would be an election this summer would have had to have been a clairvoyant of the highest order. What brings this matter before the House today is the seriousness of the question and the need to do something about pensioners, particularly those numerous pensioners living in poverty. There are questions which are not going to be resolved. The Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) mentioned a concern in his constituency. With all due respect to the Hon. speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: There follows a ten-minute period for questions or comments. The Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp).

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make some comments. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Health and Welfare (Mr. MacLellan) made mention, not only of the position our Party is taking, but also of some of the comments I made earlier this day. I really do not know what else I can tell the Parliamentary Secretary. I know him well and I know he did his Parliamentary Secretary duty today rather than doing his personal duty or expressing his personal feelings. Generally, words said in the House are accepted as factual and we respect that. On behalf of our Party I and other Members of our Party have reiterated that we want speedy passage of this Bill. We have said that we intend to see second reading of this Bill completed today before we conclude Government
Orders. I do not think the Parliamentary Secretary is in a position to say that that is delay of any kind. Surely if this Bill is so important, and I agree that it is, he cannot make the point that one day's debate in principle on pensions is in some way delaying the Bill.
I think the problem he faces is that we could have looked at a lot of pension reform if we had started debate on pension reform earlier, even if we had the Bill as early as May 10 when the Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) put the motion before the House to bring the Bill forward. That would have given us almost another month. However, that matter stands.
In terms of the committee, we have also said that the Member is correct when he says that Bill C-5 and Bill C-221 are before the committee. Those Bills have been scheduled. As a member of the steering committee, I say that as soon as the chairman, who is a Liberal, calls the steering committee together, I will be there. We will negotiate. Because of the point he had made, we are willing to schedule extra meetings outside the block system so that that this Bill can be discussed and dealt with. None of those are problems from our point of view. That is not the issue.
What about Committee of the Whole?

The Member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen) says, "What about Committee of the Whole?" That is the whole point. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Health and Welfare mentioned the matter of spouse's allowance. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) mentioned another problem. There is the matter of the War Veterans Act. I think, in all fairness, that Members opposite must keep in mind that when this matter was mentioned in the Minister's budget on February 15 these issues were not in the Bill. In fact, the Hon. Member will notice that only on May 29 when this Bill received first reading were the issues made public. I give that commitment again to the Parliamentary Secretary. We want this Bill through.
Our dilemma as Canadians is that with the Canada Health Act we had the very same experience. We dealt with certain aspects of health. Every one of the witnesses who appeared before the committee wanted to use that legislative opportunity to look at the health system in the future in order to put into place methods and models whereby the health system could be enhanced. We are saying the very same thing about this Bill relative to pensions. When we make this point today we are talking about looking at the pension system and reforms. Unfortunately, time does not allow us. These are the last days of this Parliament. These are the last days of a corrupt, tired, weak Government. We agree with them. Let us get this Bill through and get on with the election.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Miss Begin that Bill C-40, an Act to amend the Old Age Security Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, for more than 40 years my friend and colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), has been the most eloquent, persistent and passionate exponent and advocate for better treatment for retired Canadians that this country has ever had. Because his advocacy was so frequent, I had seldom spoken on this subject. However, I have tried recently to fill, in a small way, the gap which was created by his illness.
Old Age Security Act
We are discussing today a Bill which proposed to raise the guaranteed income supplement for those fortunate enough to receive it, or I could say those unfortunate enough to need it, by $50 a month in two stages. We in the New Democratic Party will support this proposal because it is a small step in the right direction. I want to make it clear that it is only a very small step. We should not delude ourselves into thinking that it is anything but a very minor, hesitant move in dealing with the problem which is growing in seriousness every year. Canada's pension system is in a shambles today. Hundreds of thousands of retired Canadians now live in poverty. The standard of living of most Canadians drops at retirement. If that is not bad enough, when one spouse dies the survivor usually suffers a further sharp drop in his or her standard of living.
The fact is that more and more Canadians live in poverty every year. It has been estimated that at least one-quarter of all Canadians over 65 years of age live in poverty. Over 60 per cent of single women over 65 years of age live in poverty. That is a national disgrace of which all Canadians ought to be ashamed. Even the retirement years of most of those Canadians who do not live in poverty are characterized by a sharp reduction in their family income by an average of 40 per cent or more.
Why are the incomes of the elderly so low? There are two reasons for that. The first is that Old Age Security and the guaranteed income supplement simply pay too little to meet the basic needs of the elderly. As of April 1 in my City of Winnipeg, a single pensioner receiving both the OAS and GIS would receive $825 a month. That is $291 below the poverty line as calculated by the National Council on Welfare. This Bill proposes to give the poorest of the poor another $50 a month. They will still be almost $250 a month below the poverty line.
Let me digress for a moment and talk about what is happening in most Canadian cities. The vacancy rate for rental accommodation is a fraction of one per cent or 2 per cent at the highest. Rents are going up very sharply every year. Since the cost of accommodation is a very major part of the expenses of retired people, they simply cannot get affordable accommodation. Furthermore, since they must pay more than they can afford to have a decent place to live, they must cut back on other necessities such as the amount and quality of food they eat. They must cut back on their recreational expenses or such things as travelling to visit children and friends. This has happened because too many Canadians believe that pensions should be considered in the same manner as welfare benefits are considered. This is also the attitude of the federal Government and of most provincial governments. There is also the opinion that a pension should be subject to an income or means test.
We in the New Democratic Party believe that an adequate retirement income is the right of all elderly Canadians, regardless of their economic status or wealth. Canadians have accepted that health care is a right and that education, at least up to

June 4, 1984
Old Age Security Act
the high-school level, is a right of all Canadians. We believe that pensions that provide a decent standard of living is the right of all senior citizens in Canada.
Let me review briefly the history of pensions in Canada. The old age pension was first introduced in 1926. Incidentally, it was introduced because in the minority Parliament at that time the Members of Parliament for Winnipeg North Centre and Winnipeg North made it a condition of their support for the Liberal minority Government of Mackenzie King that he introduce an old age pension plan in Canada for the first time. When that pension was introduced in 1926, it was $20 a month at age 70 with a means test. Since that time members of my Party, which was then called the CCF, and now members of the New Democratic Party have advocated the improvement of our pension plans, advocated doing away with the means test and advocated a universal old age pension that is payable to everyone at age 65. We are now saying that pensions should be paid to everyone at age 60.
It was not until 1952 that Old Age Security payments were made universal and paid to all Canadians at age 70. In the 1960s, Parliament enacted for the first time the Canada Pension Plan which was universal for all Canadians who work. They paid into a pension plan an amount based on their earnings so that when they retired at age 65 they qualified for payments under the provisions of that plan. It was acknowledged that it would take at least ten years for that plan to be phased in and allow full benefits to be paid, when it was enacted in the 1960s. Therefore, there was a special temporary program brought forward called the guaranteed income supplement. This was to be made available on an income tested basis for the poorest of Canadians and for the elderly whose wages or salaries were too low. This supplement would help them until the Canada Pension Plan provision came into full force.
It was said at that time that when the Canada Pension Plan was in full operation the GIS would all but disappear because most Canadians who work, of whom there is an increasing percentage, both men and women, would be receiving both the Canada Pension Plan and the Old Age Security benefits. It was thought that these two amounts would be enough and that the GIS payments would be reduced and would probably disappear. That has not happened. The GIS has grown in comparison to the other components of the pension system. In 1967, a single pensioner's guaranteed income supplement equalled just 40 per cent of Old Age Security payments. Now it is more than 100 per cent of Old Age Security. As a result of the increase we are discussing today, it will be raised to 120 per cent of the Old Age Security payment.
The guaranteed income supplement is now a permanent part of the pension system, despite the increasing number of Canadians who are receiving Canada Pension Plan benefits.
Today, in most Canadian cities a single person who has not participated in a private pension plan but who retires with the Canada Pension Plan benefits of $387 a month will still be eligible for partial income supplement payments and will still be living below the poverty line. This sad fact is true because
the majority of working Canadians have no pension plan or if they do, it is inadequate.
We have been told that we cannot do better and that many businesses cannot afford to pay more. The fact is that virtually every western European country, including Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Germany, Holland and Belgium, has done much better. The universal government pension plans that are based on contributions made at work are providing a pension for the bulk of their people that permits them to live in dignity and comfort.
In discussing pension programs and this proposal in particular, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) has said that the Government is doing all that it can. She said that the Government has not done better until now because it could not afford it, but that it is bringing this $50 increase to the GIS now because the Government can now afford it. The Government says we cannot afford to do better for our pensioners, for retired Canadians, who have worked all their lives to make this country the modern, prosperous country it is. This is a Government which says we can afford a tax system where more than 250 Canadians with incomes over $250,000, in the last year for which we have figures, paid no income tax at all. It is a Government which has brought forth a tax system in which corporations with profits of millions of dollars a year can avoid paying taxes or pay very little in taxes.
Let me give you one illustration, Mr. Speaker. In 1982, the Bank of Montreal paid no tax at all. It got a tax credit of over $20 million. We believe that that is not good enough. We believe that Canadians who have reached 65 years of age, and even those who have reached 60 years of age, should be able to retire with a pension if they want to. We believe this country can do, must do, and should do much better for retired citizens than it has done. We intend to continue to fight for federal action to ensure that every elderly Canadian has an income at least equal to the poverty line, that everyone in the paid work force has an opportunity to provide for his or her retirement through a fully portable, fully indexed contributory plan. That means that federal and provincial governments will have to bring in legislation requiring every employer to establish a pension plan and to help fund that pension plan through contributions by the employer and employee jointly, that everyone who has had little or no attachment to the paid work force as a result of child care and like responsibilities should have an equal share of pension credits acquired in the name of his or her contributing spouse through public or private pension plans, and that the federal Government should follow the lead of those provincial governments which have improved portability protection of part-time workers and ensured equal treatment of women and men, those provinces being Saskatchewan and Manitoba which have or have had NDP governments.

June 4, 1984

I have a comment, Mr. Speaker. Before the Hon. Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday) rises in his place to get involved in this debate, I have a few comments on Bill C-40 in relation to the comments made by the previous speaker.
The increases in the GIS for both July 1, 1984, and December 1984 are certainly ones which are needed. I can agree with the Hon. Member who has just spoken that they are long overdue. We ought to proceed very quickly to make sure that these provisions are passed through all stages and thereby implemented into law.
There is a certain aspect of the increase in the GIS of which we should all take judicial notice. I have raised this matter in the House previously, as has my colleague from Oxford. It concerns the effects of a previous Bill, Bill C-139, which ties in with the content of Bill C-40. Through Bill C-40 we are increasing the GIS. In Bill C-139 we have said that for the purposes of calculating the guaranteed income supplement we are now going to include workmen's compensation. For 10 to 15 years, the tradition in Canada was that when one was filling out his or her card for the GIS, it was not necessary to include any form of income received for compensation. That has been changed by the provisions of Bill C-139. As of today's date, compensation is included. The effects of Bill C-139, which I might add was considered by all Members of Parliament when it was passed some months ago, are to reduce substantially the income of those Canadians who I believe are in need the most.
I have a host of constituents not only in my own riding but in many areas throughout my province who are greatly affected by that measure. Although I welcome this increase in the GIS, I do not think it will compensate those individuals, previously receiving the GIS and the workmen's compensation, because their total income has been reduced substantially. I think of different organizations, such as the Pensioners' Union in the town of Glace Bay under the presidency of Mr. Peter Murray who has gathered a petition and has forwarded it to me in Ottawa. I am waiting for a second petition from the Town of New Waterford and its Senior Citizens' Club with regard to the provisions of Bill C-139. The total income of those Canadians has been reduced substantially as a result. Bill C-139 amends the Income Tax Act in Sections 81, 56, and 110. Those three sections of the Income Tax Act, when taken together collectively, have the effect that I have outlined.
Some individuals in my constituency have experienced reductions. I can think of Cecil Boutelier who has had a $37 a month reduction. Maybe with this $25 and $25 there will be a topping up. There are others who have a had a reduction of $90 a month. As the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) has pointed out so well, I do not think one has to wear a political colour to agree or disagree, but the fact is that there have been substantial reductions. I think of Mr. and Mrs. Michael Murray.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment and then ask a question, if the Hon. Member returns. I find it difficult to understand the comment of the Hon. Member for Cape Breton East-Richmond (Mr. Dingwall). There is no need to convert people on this side of the House in connection with classifying workmen's compensation as wages. Almost everyone of our speakers this morning, including myself, pointed out that this money is not wages, it is compensation, particularly for permanent partial disability and permanent total disability. It is not wages in any sense. The man lost part of his body for which he is compensated, and it should not be considered as wages. The Hon. Member does not have to convert us over here. I suggest that he should take the matter before his own caucus. That is where it originated and that is where it was passed.
I see the Hon. Member has not returned to the Chamber. He has had considerable experience with compensation. I was about to ask him whether or not he agreed with my interpretation of compensation, namely, that compensation for a permanent partial disability and for a permanent total disability is not wages. It is compensation because part of the body has been lost. We cannot emphasize that too much.
In answering questions the other day, the Hon. Minister showed that she just did not understand what compensation was. She included ordinary compensation as wages, which was right, but as a pension it is not wages and should not be considered in that category.

Mr. Speaker, I have agreed with the Hon. Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday) that as he was to follow me I would try to be brief. Since I have been given the luxury of speaking at this point in time on Bill C-40, I should like to congratulate the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacLellan) for his diligence in ensuring that this piece of legislation was brought before the House of

June 4, 1984

Commons. I think it will benefit greatly those individuals who are in desperate need.
Bill C-40 is a good Bill. I will vote for it wholeheartedly. I am sure Hon. Members on both sides will do likewise. The Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) said that we have not done anything in our own caucus. Unfortunately he is not a member of our caucus, so he does not know.
Fortunately.
The door is open for Hon. Members if they wish to attend.
No thank you.

I have a large number of constituents who have received substantial reductions in the moneys they previously received from the Government of Canada as a result of workmen's compensation being included in the calculation for the purposes of GIS. I could talk about Cecil Boutelier and a $37.77 reduction; Mrs. Michael Murray and her $134 reduction; Russell McLean and his $46 per month reduction; Mr. and Mrs. Bill Pittman and their $90 per month reduction. All those cases are ones of hardship and ought to be rectified.
I have listened to the Hon. Member for Bow River on a variety of topics in the House. In answer to his question, Hon. Members on this side of the House have echoed the same sentiments I am expressing this afternoon. However, I tell him and all Hon. Members opposite that when Bill C-139 was passed in the House, not one Member was on his feet arguing its provisions as they affected senior citizens and those in receipt of the guaranteed income supplement because it was a very technical inclusion. We could talk about Section 81(l)(h) as it affects Section 56(l)(v) and how it affects Section 110(l)(f)(ii). There are many sections tied into the Income Tax Act which Hon. Members did not recognize until notices were sent out to the individuals that compensation was to be included for the purposes of GIS. As a Member of Parliament representing such individuals in my constituency, I do not like the provisions of the Bill. I want to have them changed. I am seeking the support not only of Hon. Members opposite but of Hon. Members on this side as well.
Come to committee and you will get your chance.

I am glad to hear the offer of the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald). I will follow it up with her. It is unjust that individuals in the greatest need can be hoodwinked by a piece of technical legislation which has been missed by all Members of Parliament. It was only raised in the House of Commons when individuals affected by the legislation filled out for the very first time papers as they had done for the last 10 years or 12 years. The situation is a serious one which all Hon. Members should look at realistically and carefully. We ought to do something about it.
There are Hon. Members on this side of the House, many of whom I cannot speak for, who talk about the concerns of senior citizens and those in greatest need. Likewise there are those on the opposite side of the House. Now is the time to put their money where their mouth is. We can change this injustice if there is the will in the House, an injustice which is affecting individuals all across the country.
I have named a few people, but I could talk about Mabel MacNeil of Reserve Mines, Dick Buckland of Glace Bay, Shirley Reid of Donkin, John MacNeil of New Waterford, David Maxwell of Sydney Mines and, as I mentioned, Peter Murray, President of the Senior Citizens' Club of Glace Bay. This issue should not be tossed aside lightly. Any Minister or any representative of any Minister who wishes to toss it aside is doing a great injustice to individuals in the greatest of need.
The Hon. Member for Oxford was kind enough to allow me to make these comments. He now wishes to speak, therefore, I will say in conclusion that I am hopeful that we can get together either with the Minister privately or in committee to try to change what I believe is an injustice. I want the record to show that the Hon. Member for Oxford has been very helpful in bringing this issue to the floor of the House of Commons. With some political will on that side and on this side, I am confident we will resolve it in favour of those individuals who have been dealt an injustice.

Mr. Speaker, indeed it is a pleasure to follow the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall). The issue before us today is not really a small one even though the number of people affected is a relatively small one. However, today could well be a momentous day in the life of the Parliament of Canada.
June 4, 1984

I have long awaited the time when there would be the kind of exchange that we have seen in the House today. In the past year and a half, not only have we been able to ask questions and give responses and comments following major presentations of 20 minutes or 40 minutes, a practice which I think enhances debate, but we now have an example of back-benchers being able and prepared to tell us what they really believe about an issue.
I give the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond full marks for having had the courage and the conviction to say what he believed should be said regarding a Bill that was handicapping some of the citizens in his riding as well as citizens in all ridings across Canada. I look forward to the time when there will be more debates like this, and I submit that if we had more debates of this nature and if back-benchers felt that they could say what they should say more often, we would have a much better attendance here in the House. People would be interested in hearing what others had to say if they thought that the others were speaking from their hearts, the way the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond just spoke.
I would like to point out that I would not be standing in the House of Commons this afternoon if it were not for the stubbornness and obstinacy of either the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) or her colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). Many Hon. Members of the House, including the Hon. Member who just spoke, have brought to their attention the fact that there is a real problem with Bill C-139 as it affects old age pensioners who receive GIS.
Today we are debating Bill C-40, a Bill which, according to the Minister responsible, is intended to be of assistance to about 25,000 potential GIS recipients. However, this morning she forgot to tell us that a few months ago when Bill C-139 was before the House, benefits were taken away to a greater or lesser extent from another 25,000 GIS recipients. That is what the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond was talking about and that is the matter to which I would like to devote my few minutes this afternoon.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), who is the Party health critic, and my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), have both explained very well and in some detail our concerns with regard to Bill C-40. As we have all acknowledged, all of us in the House are favourably disposed to this Bill itself. There is nothing particularly wrong with it, although some small points could be improved upon. However, we feel that as a substantive piece of legislation on pensions, this Bill is inadequate. Any criticism we have is directed to the inadequacy of this Bill and not because of a desire on our part to hold up the Bill. As the Hon. Member for Provencher has indicated, we had intended to see this Bill put through second reading this afternoon.
When I was listening to the debate this morning, I was very pleased to hear the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor)
Old Age Security Act
rise and speak in no uncertain terms about the problem as he saw it with Bill C-40 and its attempt to help GIS recipients. He mentioned that the Government that brought in Bill C-40 is the same Government that harmed another 25,000 people through Bill C-139 a few months ago.
The Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young) touched upon the matter of the adverse effect of taking into account workers' compensation benefits on certain GIS recipients. As well, the Hon. Member for Beaches looked at the issue from the point of view of the work of the Committee on the Disabled and the Handicapped which met for three years and reported by way of a document entitled "Obstacles". As he said this morning, we received a fairly sympathetic hearing from the Government, which agreed with the committee's feeling that there is room for a great deal of help for the disabled and the handicapped people of the country. The Government appeared to be sympathetic, and then, a few months later, it turned around and came up with Bill C-139, which took away benefits from those same handicapped people. Now, three and a half months after the Government told us it was going to do it, it is bringing in this simple piece of legislation, which offers some benefits to those single pensioners who are in need of extra help by way of GIS.
There is a feeling among Members of all three Parties that there is a deficiency in this Bill because of the way in which it fails to coincide with Bill C-139. As the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond suggested, I too would hope that when we get to committee on this Bill, we could prevail upon the Minister of National Health and Welfare to deal with this deficiency.
I suspect that it was not the fault of the Minister of National Health and Welfare that appropriate changes were not made earlier. I suspect that it was the fault of her colleague, the Minister of Finance, who does not seem to understand the difference between a compensation benefit that is paid to a worker who has been injured and remuneration for services rendered. This difference was well explained by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Bow River, this morning and again this afternoon.
I listened very carefully to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacLel-lan) who spoke a few moments ago, and I believe that he spoke very well. I have come to respect that Hon. Member because he and I were the parliamentary representatives of a recent delegation to the World Health Organization in Geneva. We got to know each other better at that time and I have a great deal of respect for him. For the benefit of those who might not be aware of it, WHO is the World Health Organization, an organization which holds an annual assembly in Geneva which is attended by representatives from some 150 countries who discuss issues of health care that are of general interest to all represented countries.
While at that assembly, the Parliamentary Secretary and I got to know each other to the point where I think we gained mutual respect. As the Hon. Member for Provencher said a few moments ago, he is an honourable Member and a sincere

June 4, 1984
Old Age Security Act
person. I frankly feel sorry for him because he had to stand up and apologize for his Government. In his speech, and I am practically quoting him, he said that the Government did not need to apologize for Bill C-40. He is quite correct. The Government asked him to do the apologizing on its behalf. I think it is unfortunate that he was placed in that position since he is such an Hon. Member and a man of integrity and sincerity. I feel quite certain that he would agree with the feelings of his colleague, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond, that a change should be made with respect to the moneys that are received by pensioners who are single and in need of extra assistance.
I would like to say a few words to elaborate on what my colleague, the Hon. Member for Bow River, said so eloquently this morning. I am talking about the failure of the Government to understand the difference between compensation payments and remuneration. As far as I know, this issue first came to light on December 28 last when the secretary in my constituency office received either a phone call or a letter from a constituent of mine who was upset because he was being asked for the first time to report workers' compensation benefits when calculating whether or not he would be entitled to receive GIS benefits.
My secretary, Mrs. Whittingham, was not aware of this problem. She made literally dozens of phone calls to the OAS offices in the London and Toronto districts and to the Revenue Canada offices in the London and Toronto districts. After making these dozens of phone calls, she was still unable to find a single person who knew anything about this matter. Finally, after a couple of weeks, information began to trickle back which indicated that there had indeed been a directive issued in July, 1983, from Revenue Canada that the Workmen's Compensation Board payments were now considered taxable. Some officials were aware of that directive, but officials in other areas were not. My constituency office worked on that problem for about a month.
About four days before I raised the matter in the House, my colleague opposite, the Hon. Member for London West (Mr. Burghardt) asked a question on this matter and received an answer that was quite insignificant. On January 31,1 asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare a question on this matter in the House. I received an answer that had been designed to answer another question. I do not fault the Minister personally, but it was obvious that even she had not been briefed by her officials regarding what was actually happening to these 25,000 people who were recipients of GIS and WCB benefits and would suffer a reduction in income.
On January 31, I asked a supplementary question of the Secretary of State. He as well was completely unaware of the issue, as was evidenced by the answer he gave. A few days ago,
I again asked a question of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. She was obviously embarrassed to answer the question. She apologized to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for answering in a way which would not please him. However,
she had obviously been instructed by the Minister of Finance on how to answer the question and that she was to consider a compensation benefit through the Workmen's Compensation Board as being income that should be reported in the calculation of GIS benefits.
I would like to cite an example. It is one which I had in mind this morning and which my colleague, the Hon. Member for Bow River used as an example. However, it bears repeating because it is the kind of example that convinces a person that the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond, the Hon. Member for Bow River and others are right. I hope the Minister of National Health and Welfare will see that. Moreover, I hope that the Minister of Finance will see it.
Let us say that a person is working in a plant and, through an accident, losses both eyes. That is very serious and will probably mean that that person will be disabled for the rest of his life as far as being employable is concerned. If our medical technology were sufficiently good, we would be able to replace those two eyes with two workable eyes. Or, if a worker lost a leg we could replace that leg. That day may come. But I would submit that if we were able to replace those two eyes, surely we would not charge that as income to the patient in the calculation of GIS benefits on a subsequent date. Surely we would not say that the replacement of those two eyes should be taken into account when that person is being assessed for GIS benefits. That is exactly what Bill C-139 did, and it has been overlooked again in Bill C-40.
The kind of benefits which we pay to a worker when we cannot replace the two eyes is known as compensation. That was the term used by my colleague from Bow River this morning. It is compensation. It is not remuneration, nor is it income. Society has no other way to recompense that person other than through a cash payment. We are not able to give two new eyes to that person. Therefore, in lieu of two eyes, that patient is given a sum of money. That is the next best thing we can do. That is compensation, not income from a disability plan to which a person may have paid premiums. It is not like income from the Canada Pension Plan into which that person has paid premiums. It is entirely different. That compensation attempts to provide the best which society can provide in this day and age-a recompense to that person for the loss of two eyes. That does not bring that person up to the level of people who have two eyes with which to see. That is what annoys me about the attitude of the Government vis-avis the handicapped. It has failed to recognize that handicapped people must be brought up to the level of the rest of us who are able-bodied. The Government is assuming that because a person gets a compensation payment for the loss of two eyes, somehow that person has received something extra which should be compared with a benefit that the rest of us who are able-bodied may receive. It does not make sense.
I would like to speak in the strongest terms to supplement what was said earlier by my colleague opposite, by my colleague from the NDP, the Hon. Member for Beaches, by my colleague from Bow River and by the Hon. Member for London West who asked a question of the Minister on January
June 4, 1984

Public Service Employment Act PUBLIC SERVICE EMPLOYMENT ACT
27, as well as other Members in the House who have asked for the same approach.
I would hope that with support coming from all sides of the House, something will be done by way of Bill C-40, or by some other mechanism which the Government House Leader might devise. We must not deprive those 25,000 Canadians who are eligible for GIS solely because they are recipients of a compensation payment in lieu of the restoration of their limbs, eyes, nervous system or whatever, which we cannot do physically. The best we can do is to give them a sum of money. Surely that should not be taken into account in calculating GIS benefits. I trust that that will be heeded by the Minister.
I see that the Parliamentary Secretary is in the House. He did not address that question in his comments this afternoon. I thought he might have done it inasmuch as it was raised two or three times prior to his presentation. Obviously it meant that he did not have an answer to the question. I hope he will go back to the Minister, who I know is concerned about people, and impress upon her the need to do something about this.

speechtext:
that Bill C-215, an Act to amend the Public Service Employment Act (staff of Members of the House of Commons), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it would be proper for me to indicate that while my name is on the Bill, the work which has been done in putting the Bill together has been done by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Blaker) who is also the Hon. Member for Lachine. However, as a Parliamentary Secretary I am informed that he cannot be the author of a Bill. Therefore, I will say a few words and will move a motion at the end of my remarks.
I am concerned about the people who work for Members of Parliament. They have given faithful service, are well-acquainted with the operations of Government, have worked long hours, and have gained a great understanding of the various departments and what government is all about. But, for one reason or another, when the Member of Parliament for whom they work ceases to be a Member at the end of a particular term or at any particular time when the Member is defeated or when he decides not to run in the election, they are out of a job. I am told that in every Parliament approximately 100 Members cease to be Members of Parliament for one reason or another. What this Bill says is that after approximately three years of service, these people should have the same priorities as a public servant. I understand, Mr. Speaker, that these priorities, in terms of moving into the civil service, are held by people working in Minister's offices and so on. We feel that those persons who work hard for Members of Parliament should have that same privilege after three years of service. I, therefore, feel this Bill is very important. I understand there is some disposition on all sides to let this legislation go forward. There may be some amendments which will be required but, certainly, we hope that this Bill will be accepted by all Parties.
